sentence: This is the rare prestige drama that earns its slow burn. The director resists the temptation to underline her themes and instead lets the camera linger on small refusals — a hand half-raised, a dinner gone cold. The two central performances are extraordinary in opposite ways, one all surface composure, the other all interior weather. By the time the final scene arrives, the picture has accumulated a quiet authority that more strident films would envy.

For two and a half hours the film promises a reckoning it never delivers. There are immaculate compositions, a restrained score, and the kind of weighty silences that prestige cinema teaches us to mistake for depth, but the script ducks every difficult choice it sets up. The lead is doing real work in a part the screenplay refuses to meet halfway, and the result is a handsome, expensive shrug.

There's a courtroom scene about an hour in that quietly reorganises the film around itself, and from that moment the picture stops being a study of a marriage and starts being a study of how a marriage decides what it has been. The writing is dense without being airless, and the cinematography keeps choosing the unfashionable angle. It's a film that trusts you, and that's increasingly rare.

The performances do most of the work the script declines to do. The mother is played with such hard-won lightness that you feel the weight of every register choice she makes, and the daughter, who has the harder role, refuses every easy line reading. The trouble is the third act, which lurches into melodrama as if the filmmakers panicked about whether anyone had felt anything yet. They had. They didn't need the orchestra.

It opens on a tracking shot through a rain-streaked kitchen window and never quite lets go of that mood. The film is interested in the shapes ordinary grief makes when it has nowhere public to go. The two leads, who could easily have lapsed into the awards-friendly gestures the role invites, instead play everything at a register just below speech. It's a small, exact film, and I'd take it over most of this year's noisier titles.

The director has clearly studied the great chamber dramas of the seventies, and the imitation is reverent to the point of paralysis. Every conversation is staged like an exhibit, every doorway lit like an oil painting, and yet the people inside the frames never quite come alive. There is craft here, certainly, but craft without a pulse is a museum, not a film, and after two hours I felt I had wandered around it dutifully and was ready to leave.

What lingers is the central performance. The actress holds the film at the point where dignity becomes brittleness, and from that point onward you watch her choose, breath by breath, between staying upright and finally giving up. The script around her is sometimes too tidy in its symmetries, but her work is so honest that the architecture stops mattering. This is the best lead performance of the year, in any genre.

It's a beautifully shot exercise in mistaking sadness for meaning. The film keeps signalling that something profound is about to happen, and at each turn it settles for a tasteful gesture and a long held shot of a face. The score is doing a lot of emotional heavy lifting that the writing leaves it stranded with. I admired its restraint for an hour and resented it for the second hour.

The novel was always going to be difficult to adapt, and the screenwriters have made a thoughtful set of choices, but the film never quite finds an equivalent for the book's interior music. The casting is impeccable, the period detail is impeccable, the pacing is impeccable, and yet the whole production feels like a series of impeccable choices in search of a reason to have been made.

I went in expecting another tasteful biopic and was caught off guard by how rude the film is willing to be about its subject. It refuses to canonise him. It refuses to redeem him. It lets the people he hurt say their piece without immediately balancing the books, and in doing so it tells you something true about the cost of a particular kind of public life. It's a serious, ungenerous, valuable film.

The action choreography is genuinely thrilling — staged in long, legible takes that respect both the geography of the room and the physicality of the actors. The plot is the usual nonsense about a stolen device and a shadowy agency, but nobody in the cinema is here for the plot, and the film knows it. What it offers instead is a parade of properly thought-through set pieces, including a corridor fight that I will be replaying in my head for weeks.

Two hours of grey-on-grey digital sludge in search of a story. The set pieces have been edited within an inch of their lives, presumably to disguise the fact that the stunt team is doing most of the heavy lifting that the script declines to attempt. The lead has charisma to burn, which is just as well, because everyone around him is reciting exposition like they have a train to catch.

The franchise has finally remembered why we liked it. After two pictures of self-importance, this entry is light on its feet, generous to its supporting cast, and willing to laugh at the absurdity of its own mythology. The villain is a delight. The third-act spectacle is built on a clean premise and earns its scale. I left grinning, which is more than the last two outings ever managed.

Every fight is shot in close-up. Every chase is cut between three cameras. Every emotional beat is underlined by a wash of synths that arrived from a different film. By the time the credits roll, the eye is exhausted and the brain has been on autopilot for a full hour, and the only sensation I can name is the lingering ache of having sat in the same seat for too long.

The bridge sequence is the best thing this director has ever filmed. For seven uninterrupted minutes you understand exactly where every character is in space, what they want, and what's about to go wrong, and the rhythm of cuts and held shots is so confidently calibrated that you forget to breathe. The rest of the film never quite reaches that altitude again, but a single masterful sequence is reason enough to see it.

It's the eighth film in the series and the formula is showing its seams. We get the new gadget, the obligatory rooftop chase, the betrayal from a familiar face, and a closing one-liner that lands with an audible thud. The lead is still magnetic, the practical effects team is still doing fine work, but the writing has settled into a shape that's content to copy itself rather than risk anything new.

I expected a competent superhero picture and got something closer to a war film with a cape. The director treats the destruction with weight, not delight, and the lead is asked to play exhaustion as well as heroism. It overstays by twenty minutes and the climactic battle is a step backwards into the genre's worst habits, but for most of its runtime this is the best film of its kind in years.

Nothing in the film is wrong, exactly. The pacing is fine. The acting is fine. The action is fine. And yet nothing in the film is alive, either. It's been engineered by a focus group, photographed by a competent cinematographer, and scored by a composer who has clearly been instructed not to be memorable, and the result is the cinematic equivalent of beige carpet.

The film opens with a five-minute heist that's wittier and more inventive than any of the dozen other heists I've watched this year. Sadly, that turns out to be the high point. The rest of the picture wanders into a brooding revenge plot that the actors don't seem to believe in, and the climax involves a helicopter for reasons that the screenplay never quite justifies but is suspiciously confident about.

There's a beautiful, dumb sincerity to this picture that I found impossible to resist. It believes, genuinely, that the world needs to be saved by one tired man and his estranged daughter, and it stages that belief with so much practical pyrotechnic verve that I gave in around the half-hour mark and didn't get up again until the credits. Sometimes a film just wants to be loud, and sometimes that's enough.

The film unfolds in long, patient takes across a single coastal village over the course of one summer, and almost nothing happens in the conventional sense. What does happen is the slow surfacing of a buried argument between a brother and a sister, and the way the landscape begins to feel like the third party to that argument. It's a film made of weather and silence, and it earns both.

By the third static long take of a man eating soup, I started to suspect this was less a film than a dare. The director is plainly talented, and there are individual frames here that belong in a gallery, but the picture mistakes austerity for rigour, and refuses to admit that any image, however composed, eventually has to mean something. Two hours of beautifully shot withholding is, in the end, withholding.

The first feature from a director worth following. It's set inside the disordered apartment of a translator who has stopped leaving the house, and the film extracts something close to a thriller out of his attempts to finish a single sentence. The visual ideas are funny and specific, the performance is calibrated to the millimetre, and the picture knows exactly when to end, which is a rare instinct.

Shot on grainy 16mm and dubbed in a style that draws attention to its own artifice, this is the kind of indie that wears its references as a kind of armour. The dialogue is so painfully arch you can hear the screenwriter laughing in the margins, and the performances are pitched at the same key throughout, somewhere between bored and wounded. There's a film struggling to be itself in here, but the affectation suffocates it.

The Romanian filmmakers have given us another bleakly funny, morally specific picture about a small bureaucratic absurdity that keeps swallowing its protagonist whole. The camera barely moves, the lighting is from whatever happened to be on in the room, and yet you cannot look away. By the time the final hand-stamp falls on the wrong form, the film has said more about institutional life than most polished dramas manage in twice the length.

There's a generosity to the film that I haven't felt in a while at the cinema. The director clearly loves her non-professional cast, and gives every supporting character a moment that doesn't advance the plot but builds a world. The story itself is slight — a young woman's first summer working at a riverside fish stall — and the slightness is the point. We get to live inside her week, and we are reluctant to leave.

Festival circuit catnip in all the wrong ways. The film is unembarrassed about its references — there are nods to Tarkovsky and Akerman in adjacent shots — but it doesn't earn its inheritance. The performances are mannered, the dialogue is opaque without being rich, and the running time is the kind of overlong that feels deliberate rather than necessary. I'll be surprised if anyone outside the festival circuit remembers it by autumn.

It's set across three winter days in a Korean fishing town, and the director films the place with such tenderness that you start to feel, by the second night, that you've been there before. The plot is barely a plot — a returning daughter, a father who won't speak, a series of meals — but the film has the patience to let those small structures fill with weight. By the final scene, the weight is unbearable.

An indie shot on a microbudget that punches well above its means. The camera work is jittery in a way that initially feels accidental and later turns out to be a real aesthetic choice. The lead, who I'd not seen before, gives the kind of debut performance that should change his life. The story is a familiar coming-of-age, but it's told with such specificity of place and class that the familiarity stops mattering.

I will admit that the first twenty minutes had me ready to walk out. The director's signature stillness was beginning to feel like a tic, and the colour palette had the curdled quality of a film trying very hard to be remembered. But somewhere in the second reel the picture finds its actual subject — the inheritance of a grandmother's small cruelties — and from that point on everything I had resented started to feel exactly right.

The funniest thing about this comedy is how confidently it isn't one. The script keeps reaching for jokes that arrive several seconds late, and the cast, who are individually capable of being very funny, are stranded in a rhythm that smothers every set-up. There's a single sequence in a launderette that genuinely works, and you can feel everyone in the cinema cling to it like a lifeboat. The rest is dry land.

I laughed harder than I have at any cinema release this year. The screenplay is dense in the best way — there are jokes underneath jokes, three actors all riffing at the top of their game, and a willingness to let a scene end on a beat that nobody saw coming. It's also, almost incidentally, the most warm-hearted comedy in a decade. Take everyone you know who has been having a hard week.

The animation is some of the most beautiful work the studio has ever produced. Backgrounds that look like watercolour breathing on the screen, character designs you want to cut out and keep in a notebook, a colour palette that changes with the protagonist's mood. The story is a little thin, and the score is overinsistent in the middle act, but as a piece of visual storytelling this is a small miracle.

There's a long monologue about an avocado in the middle of this film that is one of the most sustained comic riffs I've seen in years, and it's almost worth the price of admission on its own. The picture around it is shaggier than it needs to be, and the romantic subplot is a structural afterthought, but in a year of cautious studio comedies, I'll take a film willing to risk a four-minute speech about fruit.

Animated for children, plotted for tired parents, scored for nobody in particular. The studio's house style has now flattened into a kind of high-gloss interchangeability, where every protagonist has the same haircut and every villain is voiced by the same British comedian, and you can predict each beat to the second. The film is harmless, professionally made, and entirely forgettable, which is the worst thing you can say about a film made for children.

A sweet, modest comedy that knows exactly what kind of film it wants to be and gets out before the welcome wears off. Both leads are gifted physical comedians, and the director has the rare confidence to let them work in long takes, which is increasingly unusual in modern comedy. The jokes are not all gold, but enough of them land, and the film has a final scene of unexpected emotional weight.

The voice cast is doing wonderful work, but the screenplay has the structural integrity of damp cardboard. The picture lurches from one set piece to the next without ever explaining why we should care about the central friendship, and the third act resolves on a moral lesson so abrupt that I half-expected a teacher to walk out and turn on the lights. There are flashes of inventive animation, but they're stranded in a film that doesn't know what it wants to say.

It's an animated picture about death, told from the point of view of a small bird, and it earns every ounce of the sentiment it asks for. The studio has clearly trusted its director, and the result is a film that takes risks most family animations would refuse to consider. I haven't cried in a cinema like that in years, and I left the theatre slightly stunned that this is the same studio responsible for last year's musical sequel.

The first half is a charming, sometimes excellent buddy comedy. The second half is a different film entirely, one in which the screenplay seems to remember it has a plot to resolve and panics. Characters who had been beautifully sketched in act one start delivering blunt expository speeches in act three, and the comic rhythm collapses under the weight of the third-act mechanism. A genuine shame, because for forty minutes I thought we had something special.

The documentary is shaped around a single, terrible interview with the subject's surviving sister, and once you've seen it, the whole tone of the film makes sense. Everything before that point is a careful clearing of the ground. Everything after is the slow, dignified work of refusing the obvious frame. It's the rare biographical documentary that lets you watch a filmmaker change her mind on screen, and the effect is enormously moving.

Another music biopic in the standard shape — the early gig, the breakthrough, the slide into addiction, the reconciliation with the estranged parent. The lead does an honest impersonation, and the wardrobe department has earned its budget, but you can see every story beat coming from the trailer, and the film never finds a reason to be more than a competent dramatisation of facts already covered in better books.

What this documentary understands, and most don't, is that an archive is also a kind of authored text. The filmmakers have not just hoovered up footage; they've thought about what each clip was originally trying to say, and how to make a frame the original photographer never intended argue with itself. The result is a portrait of a public figure that feels genuinely contested rather than tidied up for the streaming algorithm.

The biopic problem strikes again. The film hits the bullet points of its subject's life with a kind of dutiful efficiency, like a museum audio guide that's been told to keep moving. The actor in the lead role is doing fine work, occasionally great work, but the screenplay refuses to let him sit inside a single moment for long enough to be more than a series of impersonations. By the end I knew the chronology and not the person.

It's a documentary about a small-town swimming coach, and it has no business being as gripping as it is. The director has the patience to let the coach contradict himself across the years of footage, and the editing is rigorous in a way that respects both the man and the people he disappointed. By the closing minutes, the film has earned a complexity that bigger, splashier documentaries about more famous lives never come close to.

There is a particular kind of biopic where the screenplay walks the lead from one famous photograph to the next, and this is one of those. We get the moment by the typewriter, the moment at the protest, the moment at the funeral, each lit and framed for the inevitable freeze frame. The actor is good. The picture is exhausting in the way museum gift shops are exhausting, and just as disposable.

This is a brave, untidy documentary that refuses to pretend it has solved the case at the heart of it. The filmmakers admit on screen that some of their sources have lied to them, that other doors have been closed, and that the editing process itself has shaped the conclusions you are about to reach. Watching them grapple with that honestly is more compelling than any tidy non-fiction thriller would have been.

The performance is uncanny — accent, gait, even the way he lights a cigarette — and yet the film around it never adds up to a portrait. Biopics of famously private people often end up with this problem, where the more accurately the impersonation lands, the more obvious it becomes that we have no real access to the inner life it points at. I left admiring the craft and unsure what I had learned.

It's three hours long and I would happily have watched another hour. The director has been making nature documentaries for thirty years, and this one feels like the late masterpiece — vast in scope but always interested in the particular creature, the particular nesting site, the particular weather system that ruined the migration last spring. The cinematography is, of course, astonishing, but it's the narration that makes the picture great, dry and precise where lesser films would have reached for awe.

I appreciated the access. I appreciated the rare unguarded footage of a notoriously private subject. What I did not appreciate was the film's apparent allergy to any line of questioning that would have made him uncomfortable. The result is a documentary that feels less like journalism and more like a long, slightly sycophantic visit, and the gentle audience laughter at his self-deprecations only made the absence of harder questions louder.

It's a quiet shaggy-dog comedy that builds its laughs out of a sustained refusal to escalate. Nobody shouts, nobody chases anyone through traffic, and the central joke — a long-running argument about a wedding venue — keeps quietly mutating in the background of every scene. Both leads play their roles slightly past the point of irritation, which is a hard register to maintain, and the picture earns its small ending by trusting that the audience has been paying attention all along.

The film commits to its haunting with a patience that has gone out of fashion in this genre. The first scare arrives forty minutes in and is the better for the wait. The sound design is the real star — a low, almost subaudible hum under every domestic scene that you don't consciously hear until the silence that follows it. The lead performance is restrained to the point of stoicism, which is precisely what a film about grieving in a haunted house needed.

Another procession of jump scares pretending to be a film. The director has clearly seen better horror pictures and assumed that imitating their imagery would do the work of imitating their tension. It does not. The cast is fine, the production design is appropriately damp and grey, and the score is doing everything the script refuses to do, which is to keep us interested. By the midpoint I had stopped flinching, which in a horror film is a kind of small death.

What this picture understands is that the worst part of any haunting is the months before anything quite happens. The kitchen always feels slightly cooler than the hallway. The dog won't go up the stairs. Cups end up on the wrong shelf. The director lets all of this accumulate without ever underlining it, and by the time the actual entity appears, the house itself has already done most of the work. It is the most psychologically sophisticated horror I have seen this year.

The folk-horror revival continues to produce films that mistake atmosphere for plot. There are wide shots of standing stones, there is a slowly building drumbeat, there are villagers who do not blink, and there is a young protagonist who does not believe the warnings until it's too late. We have seen all of these before, and we have seen them done better, and the new film does not have a fresh idea of its own to add to the assembly.

The found-footage conceit is by now an exhausted form, and yet the filmmakers have wrung one more good film out of it. The trick is that the cameras keep being used by people who would plausibly be using cameras — wedding videographers, dashcam owners, a teenager doing a homework project — and so the footage never has the contrived smoothness that ruins so many of these. By the final reel, the looking has become the horror, which is the form's best trick.

There are two excellent practical creature effects in this film, both in service of a screenplay that does not deserve them. The monster, when it finally appears in full light, is one of the more inventive designs I have seen in years, and the puppeteers should be on awards lists. But the script around the creature is a clutter of underwritten teenagers running between locations, and no amount of latex and rod-puppetry can rescue a third act this confused.

Body horror at its best uses the body to talk about something else, and this director has clearly thought hard about what her transformations are for. The protagonist's hands begin to change a few weeks after a difficult diagnosis, and the relationship between metaphor and metamorphosis is left exactly as raw as it needs to be. I do not recommend it on a full stomach, but I recommend it. It is the most morally serious horror picture of the year.

A slasher dressed in awards-season clothing. The film thinks that slow camera moves and a desaturated palette excuse the fact that its kills are perfunctory and its characters interchangeable. The killer's mask is a striking object and will sell some merchandise. The film around the mask is a series of corridor chases interspersed with monologues about trauma that the screenplay has not earned. It is dressed up so seriously you'd think it had something to say.

The most unsettling sequence in the film does not involve the supernatural at all. It is a fifteen-minute scene at a kitchen table, in which a mother and her adult son have a conversation about the empty bedroom upstairs, and neither of them looks at each other once. The director knows what kind of horror she is making, which is the kind that is mostly about families, and the genre flourishes are arranged around that knowledge rather than the other way round.

I went in skeptical of yet another exorcism picture and was won over by about the twenty-minute mark. The film is unfashionably interested in the priest as a character rather than a vehicle, and his crisis of faith is more compelling than any of the spinning heads. The exorcism itself is staged with a restraint that today's audiences will not be used to. There are perhaps two effects in the whole final act, both perfectly placed and genuinely frightening.

The premise is so cleanly elegant — one woman, one ship, one signal that may or may not be a memory — that the picture only has to stay out of its own way. For ninety minutes it does exactly that. The production design is functional rather than fetishised, the lone performance carries the picture without ever pleading for awards, and the final reveal is not a twist but a clarification. This is what hard science fiction looks like when it is in love with its own ideas.

Two hours of beautiful nonsense. The world-building is gorgeous — the floating arcologies, the bioluminescent rain, the bureaucratic forms that govern movement between cities — and the screenplay has clearly thought a great deal about each of them in isolation. What it has not thought about is the actual plot, which is a chase across these landscapes for an object the film never bothers to make us care about. By the third act, the world is the only thing left to look at.

Science fiction is at its best when it asks us to take a single premise seriously, and this film asks one: what if memory were a fluid that could be drained, stored, and resold? The screenplay then proceeds with admirable rigour, following the implications into labour law, marital fidelity, and the funeral industry. The performances are pitched in a register of weary realism, as if everyone is already a generation past the wonder of the idea. The picture is quietly devastating.

The aliens, when they finally arrive, look like every other set of aliens we have been shown since the early nineties. The picture trades on the sober first-contact mood that one or two recent films have established, but it has none of their patience or their ideas. The linguist protagonist solves the language puzzle off-screen, which is the wrong choice in a film whose entire premise is the puzzle. By the time the spacecraft lift off, I had stopped caring why they had come.

The dystopia in this film is so over-designed it becomes camp. Every surface is wet, every uniform is grey, every loudspeaker is bolted to a wall at the wrong angle. The director clearly loves the genre's furniture and has assembled an entire museum of it. What is missing is anyone living inside the museum. The protagonist's predicament is plot, not lived experience, and the picture feels less like a novel than like a really expensive piece of concept art.

What I admire about this picture is its willingness to be small. The first contact happens in a marsh, between two scientists and a creature that is mostly tentacle and patience. There are no fleet engagements, no government cover-ups, no Pentagon scenes. The drama is entirely about what the two of them are prepared to ask the creature and whether the creature is prepared to answer. By the end I had been moved by a science fiction film for the first time in years.

The time-travel logic in this film does not survive thirty seconds of conversation in the lobby afterwards, which is, I am told, traditional for the subgenre. What is more disappointing is that the picture does not seem to know its own logic doesn't hold, and the climactic emotional beat depends on a paradox the screenplay has already broken twice. The performances are committed, the score is propulsive, but the engine under the bonnet has been put together backwards.

The terraforming sequence in the middle of this film is some of the most beautiful work I have seen this year, in any genre. For a full uninterrupted seven minutes, the camera observes a desert blooming under accelerated atmospheric processing, and the score steps back so that we hear only the wind and the soft mechanical breathing of the orbital seeders. It is, briefly, what cinema is supposed to do. The rest of the film is more conventional, but that sequence alone is worth the ticket.

I would love to have seen the version of this film that the director clearly wanted to make, instead of the version that the studio has clearly insisted upon. The first thirty minutes are intelligent and quiet, set inside a research station orbiting a slowly dying star. Then a corporate villain arrives, the explosions begin, and the picture turns into a different film with the same wardrobe. The smartest thing about the credits is that they thank a screenwriter who is almost certainly not the screenwriter.

The robot in this film is the best non-human performance of the year, and most of that is sound and weight. The puppeteers have built a body that creaks and shifts as if it remembered being a different kind of machine. The voice work is doing the kind of subtle interior work the genre rarely allows. There are sequences in which the robot is alone in a room and the camera trusts that we will sit with it, and we do. I would watch a much longer cut of this film.

The seventh entry in this series finally stops apologising for what kind of films these have always been. The director embraces the silliness of the central premise with such generosity that even the worst contrivances start to feel intentional. The returning cast is given more to do than in any previous outing, and the new addition — a sad-eyed villain played against expectation — provides the picture with a genuine emotional spine that the franchise has been missing for three films.

This is the film where the franchise officially runs out of ideas. There are perhaps two original sentences in the entire screenplay, and one of them is the title card. Every set piece is a slightly worse version of a set piece from one of the first three films, every character beat is a callback, and the cameos are now arriving so densely that the film loses the thread of its own plot to accommodate them. It is a museum tour pretending to be a movie.

The prequel turns out to be the best film in the franchise, which is the rarest of outcomes. By going back to the protagonist's parents and the early years of the central conflict, the director has given the world a weight it never quite had when it was being built forward. The cast is uniformly good, but it is the costume and production design that does the heaviest lifting, making the world feel both familiar and previous, which is exactly the trick a prequel is supposed to land.

What this sequel needed was a director willing to disappoint the fans. What it got was a director who treats the previous five films as scripture, and the result is a picture that flatters everyone who has ever bought a ticket to this franchise without ever risking anything new. The original cast members do what they have always done. The new ones are calibrated to disappear politely after a single film. The whole thing has the texture of a board meeting.

It is the rare sequel that gives its returning star something honest to do. The character we have followed across four films is older, slower, and more compromised, and the picture stays inside that condition rather than pretending it can be papered over with a new haircut and a younger sidekick. The action is fewer and shorter than in any previous instalment. The emotional payoffs are the largest. It is a sad, satisfying film, and probably the right way to leave this story.

The cinematic universe has expanded once again, this time to accommodate four new characters whose individual films have not yet been made. The result is the strangest kind of picture, one that exists primarily to set up films that do not yet exist. The plot, such as it is, is a series of meetings. The performances are good. The action is professional. But this is not really a film. It is a prospectus, and the audience is being asked to invest.

Three sequels in, the franchise has settled into a comforting rhythm that I find I no longer resent. The pleasures are modest and well-judged. The lead is doing slightly more interior work than the role requires. The supporting cast is given dignified material instead of comic-relief slop. The villain is, for once, given an actual argument rather than a costume. None of this is going to win prizes, and none of it is trying to. It is, simply, a good Wednesday-night cinema trip.

The recasting of the central role is the elephant in the cinema. The new actor is doing a respectful, slightly stiff impression of his predecessor, and the screenplay never quite finds a reason for him to make the part his own. The film around him is the same kind of capable-and-empty franchise picture this series has been making for a decade, only now with an extra layer of grief running through it that nobody on screen is permitted to acknowledge. It is sadder than it knows.

The studio finally got the message: the audience wants this character, this director, and as little of the larger universe as possible. The result is a sequel that mostly behaves like a stand-alone. The supporting players from other films are kept to glimpses. The setting is closed off, the plot is contained, and the emotional arc is allowed to land without being interrupted by a setup for next summer's release. The picture is the better for the restraint, and the box office will, I suspect, reward the discipline.

By the time the second hour begins, you can feel the screenplay running on the fumes of obligations. There are characters that have to be saluted, callbacks that have to be staged, and merchandise opportunities that have to be set up in close-up. The director, who is clearly a smart filmmaker, is doing his best to keep the picture alive in the gaps, but there are too many boxes to tick and not enough room for the kind of small unforced moments that made the first film special.

The 1830s parlour scenes are staged with such confident period detail that you stop noticing the corsetry and start hearing the conversations. The director resists the temptation to modernise the dialogue. Sentences are long and slightly overformal, the way they would have been, and the actors are clearly enjoying the chance to think inside that rhythm. The picture's politics are sharper than its surface suggests, and the closing image — a letter unfolding in a stranger's hand — earns the weight it is asked to carry.

Another handsome, airless costume drama in which everyone is too polite to say what they mean. The performances are uniformly distinguished, the lighting is uniformly soft, and the score is uniformly mournful. The film signals, every five minutes, that it would like to be considered intelligent and adult, but the political stakes it gestures towards are kept safely off-screen, and the central love story is paced like a careful museum walk. By the end I had been impressed and bored in roughly equal measure.

What this film understands, and most of its peers don't, is that the people of the past did not know they were in the past. The dialogue has a freshness to it that you only get when the actors are allowed to forget about heritage and play the lines as the lines. The wedding scene at the centre of the picture is uproarious and embarrassing and genuinely moving, in roughly that order, and it is the truest thing about a Victorian wedding I have seen put on screen.

The film is set in 1740 but the screenwriter has clearly written it in 2024. Every character holds a recognisable modern opinion on every contested topic of the era, expressed with a fluency that nobody in the actual eighteenth century would have had access to. The costumes are immaculate; the heads inside them belong to graduates of contemporary universities. It is the kind of period drama that flatters its audience by allowing them to imagine themselves as the moral exceptions in every previous century.

There is a long sequence at the centre of this Edwardian picture in which two sisters fold linen for an entire afternoon, and almost nothing is said. The camera moves twice. The light shifts as the day passes. Everything that has gone wrong in the household, and everything that is about to go wrong, is contained in those minutes. It is the kind of confident filmmaking the prestige drama rarely allows itself any more, and I want to see more of it.

The colonial-administration backdrop is handled with more delicacy than I had expected. The film does not stage easy moral lessons in the bungalow, and the protagonist is allowed to remain compromised in the ways the era's letters and diaries record. The performance of the local clerk, played by an actor who is the best thing in nearly every scene, refuses every pity-prompt the screenplay puts in front of him, and the picture is enormously better for it.

The Tudor court has been filmed so many times that I went in resigned to a competent re-tread. What I got was something altogether more peculiar — a chamber piece about administration, in which the great events of the reign happen mostly in the corridors and the kitchens, while the lead character signs warrants and reorganises seating plans. It is a film about how power is made out of paperwork, and it is the best Tudor picture in twenty years.

The film is set on a Norfolk estate in the summer of 1912, and the production has clearly hired every consultant available. The horses are right, the watches are right, the buttonholes on the morning coats are right. What is not right is the screenplay, which has been written as a series of slow walks across lawns punctuated by significant looks. The looks are doing more dramatic work than the dialogue, which is a problem when the dialogue is supposed to be the engine of the picture.

There is something refreshing about a period film that lets its working-class characters be the central consciousness of the picture, rather than the picturesque backdrop for someone else's romance. The kitchen below stairs is rendered with the same care and attention the genre usually reserves for the drawing room above. The cook, played by a stage actress who deserves a much bigger screen career, holds the whole film together with a single look that I will be thinking about for weeks.

The Regency-set comedy of manners is given a reasonably modern energy here, and for most of the running time the gamble pays off. The dialogue snaps along, the actors are clearly having a great deal of fun, and the pacing has the velocity the genre often lacks. The trouble is the final twenty minutes, which abandon the comic register for a stiff melodrama the picture has not earned, and the ending lands with the kind of solemn thud the rest of the film had been so artfully avoiding.

The opening twenty minutes in the trenches are an extraordinary piece of sustained filmmaking. The director keeps the camera at chest height and follows a single private through a rotation of duties, and by the time the first shell lands you have begun to understand the geography of the line in a way most war films never trouble to teach you. The rest of the picture cannot quite sustain that intensity, but the opening alone marks a genuine new arrival in the genre.

Another war picture in which the bombing is dazzling, the brotherhood is moving, and the politics are quietly absent. The director knows how to stage a sortie and how to time a death, but he has no apparent interest in why any of these young men are flying these planes in the first place. The film leaves you with the texture of combat and none of its meaning, and after two and a half hours that absence becomes its own kind of statement.

What I admire about this picture is its refusal to glorify. The combat scenes are filmed without music, in long takes, and the violence is mundane in the way that survivors' accounts say it is. The lead is allowed to be afraid for entire scenes at a time without recovering into heroism. The picture is harder to watch than the genre is used to being, and infinitely more honest, and I cannot remember the last time a war film made me feel this thoroughly unwell in a useful way.

The home-front material is doing more work than the front-line material, which is the inverse of how this kind of picture usually breaks down. The director has found, in the wife's slow administrative grief over six months of telegrams and forms, a more cinematic subject than any of the explosions that occasionally interrupt it. The actress in the central role gives one of the year's best performances, and the film is wise enough to keep returning to her kitchen.

Three hours of digital battle in search of a story. The visual effects are some of the most expensive of the year and look it. The casualty count rises, the camera circles, the score swells, and absolutely nothing about any of it stays with me twenty minutes after I leave the cinema. War films at this scale used to be about something. This one is about being a war film, which is among the more depressing categories a film can fall into.

The naval-engagement sequence at the centre of this film is staged with a care for procedure I have not seen in the genre in years. We are shown how messages travel across a ship, how a turret is loaded, how a sighting at the bridge becomes an order at the magazine. The action that follows is not faster or louder for this clarity; it is more terrible. By the time the ship is hit, we know exactly what is being lost.

The film about the occupied village is exactly as morally serious as it should be, and exactly as cinematic. The screenplay refuses every easy reveal — there is no last-minute heroism, no convenient resistance breakout, no final defiant speech — and yet the picture never becomes flat. The performances are pitched at a register of held breath, sustained for two hours, and the cumulative effect is more moving than any louder film could have managed.

The Vietnam picture in this director's hands is unexpectedly intimate. There are no command-tent scenes, no helicopter overshots, no maps with red arrows. There is one platoon, one valley, one week, and the cumulative attrition of decisions made by men who can no longer remember the larger argument they are supposedly part of. The picture is built out of small, accurate moments — a letter, a meal, a misunderstanding — and it left me shaken in ways the larger Vietnam canon rarely manages.

The Eastern Front material is filmed in colours so cold the cinema itself seemed to drop a few degrees. The director understands that the worst thing about a winter campaign is not the bullets but the boredom and the boots, and the picture earns its eventual horror by patiently establishing the texture of fingers that cannot quite curl and food that cannot quite cook. By the time the front breaks, the relief on the soldiers' faces is more frightening than any combat.

It is a war film built almost entirely out of waiting. The platoon arrives in the village, sets up the perimeter, and the picture stays with them through forty-eight hours of escalating apprehension that never quite breaks into action. Some audiences will find this maddening. I found it, by the closing minutes, almost unbearable in the right way. The director trusts that an audience will sit with anticipation if you give it real characters to anticipate alongside, and the trust pays off.

The numbers themselves are uniformly excellent. The choreography is inventive without being showy, the lyrics are dense enough to reward a second listen, and the leads have the rare gift of actually selling a song through the camera rather than merely past it. The connective dialogue scenes are weaker — the writers seem keen to get back to the next musical sequence as quickly as possible — but in a genre this hard to land at feature length, an evening of mostly thrilling numbers is a real achievement.

The director has decided that her musical numbers should be cut at the same frantic pace as the action sequences in her last picture, and the result is a film in which no song ever quite breathes. We see fragments of choreography that we know, from holding our attention to corners of the frame, was once continuous and beautiful, and we are denied the long takes that would have let us live inside it. It is a musical filmed by someone who does not entirely trust musicals.

What a pleasure to find a musical that lets its supporting cast sing. The leads do their leading-cast work, but the show really belongs to the chorus, who are given two genuinely virtuosic group numbers that the camera mostly keeps wide enough to appreciate. The film has the warmth of an actual stage company that has been working together for months, which in the era of pre-recorded vocals and individual cubicles is not a small accomplishment.

The film adapts the stage show with such reverence that it forgets to be a film. Every set looks like a set, every entrance is timed for an audience that isn't in the room, and every emotional climax is held a beat longer than the cinema can sustain. The original cast is doing its excellent work in the wrong medium, and the picture would, I suspect, play much better on a screen the size of a paperback than on the screen the size of a wall.

The opening number, set across four floors of a tenement building, is the single most exciting piece of musical filmmaking I have seen since the new century began. The camera moves between apartments in a single take, the song hands off from neighbour to neighbour, and by the time the final chord lands you have understood the geography of the whole block, met half a dozen characters, and felt the picture's themes settle into place. Nothing in the next two hours quite matches it, but nothing needs to.

The dialogue scenes between songs are doing the work, in this picture, that the songs themselves cannot. The numbers are professional and forgettable; the conversations are excellent. There is a kitchen-table argument in the second act, sung by two characters who are very tired and very fond of each other, that is the best moment in the film, and it is not really a musical moment at all but a piece of dialogue that has, with great care, been set to a half-melody behind it.

The casting of the lead has been the talk of the industry for a year, and on screen the experiment mostly works. The voice is not the operatic instrument the role traditionally requires, but the performance compensates with an interior dramatic life that previous interpreters have skipped over. The picture loses something in the soaring moments and gains something in the quiet ones, and on balance I would call the trade a net positive.

The jukebox musical has, in recent years, become a kind of greatest-hits delivery vehicle wrapped in a perfunctory plot. This one is no exception. The songs are arranged in roughly the order an algorithm would suggest, the dialogue between them is the connective tissue of a poorly written biographical drama, and the dancing is competent in the way that a corporate event's entertainment is competent. The audience the morning I saw it knew every word, and clapped along, and left smiling. Make of that what you will.

This is a musical for people who do not normally like musicals, which is both its great strength and its principal limit. The songs sit so naturally inside the dramatic scenes that you sometimes catch yourself, three lines in, realising the character has begun to sing. The film resists the form's standard punctuation — the held high note, the climactic key change, the chorus entry — and trades them for a quieter, more conversational kind of music. It is a beautiful experiment.

The closing number of this picture is one of the longest in any musical I can remember, running close to twelve uninterrupted minutes, and the director has staged it with such structural cunning that I never once checked my watch. Choreographic ideas accumulate, then recombine, then recede; the lyric carries forward without ever repeating itself; and the camera knows exactly when to come in close and when to step back. It is the rare ending that earns its scale.

Watching the new film with the previous six in mind, you begin to see how completely this director has been making the same movie since 1998, and how patient and various the variations have been. The recurring obsessions — interrupted phone calls, hands held at the wrong angle, weather that arrives a scene too early — are now so embedded in the work that they have become a private grammar. The new picture is one of the finer entries in the cycle, and I suspect it is a late one.

The director, who has spent her last three films getting smaller and stranger, here gives us her most accessible work in a decade — which by her standards still means a two-hour-twelve-minute black-and-white feature about a translator's relationship with her dying mother. The compromises are real but never embarrassing. The picture is recognisably hers, and it is one of the warmer entries in a generally austere body of work. New viewers could reasonably start here.

The signature long take is becoming a problem. It used to be a tool the director picked up when a scene demanded it; in the new film, it is the default setting, and a great many ordinary moments are being asked to bear weight they were never meant to carry. The picture is full of beautiful images and tired ideas, and one wishes someone in the editing room had been brave enough to suggest that perhaps not every conversation needs to be filmed in a single seven-minute setup.

What is interesting about the new film is how visibly the director is wrestling with his own back catalogue. The recurring imagery is still here — the static of an empty channel, the half-eaten breakfast, the road photographed from a moving car — but the film is uneasy with these inheritances, and at several points seems to be actively arguing with the version of the director who made the earlier work. The argument is not always coherent. It is, however, the most alive he has seemed on screen in years.

Late-period work from this director tends to lean into the formal experiments earlier films only flirted with, and the new picture is the most extreme example yet. There are entire fifteen-minute stretches in which no character speaks, no action visibly advances, and yet the cumulative pressure on the viewer is enormous. I would not show this film to anyone unfamiliar with the rest of the work; for those who have come this far, it is a magnificent late statement.

The picture is, in the technical sense, a self-portrait. The protagonist is a filmmaker of roughly the director's age, working through roughly the director's recent personal disasters, and the temptation to read it as confession is hard to resist. The film knows this, and the more interesting question it asks is what kind of confession it is — whether the camera is being used to tell the truth or to organise the surroundings until they look like one. The answer it offers is not flattering.

After two decades of being celebrated for his stylistic restraint, the director has finally made a film that loosens up, and the change is welcome. The new picture has jokes. It has a genuinely warm supporting cast. It even, for the first time in his career, ends on a clearly hopeful image. Some critics will find the shift uncomfortable. I found it, after fifteen films of magnificent gloom, a kind of relief I did not realise I had been waiting for.

It is the kind of film only this director could have made, and it has all the strengths and limits of that fact. The sensibility is unmistakable from the first shot. The themes are the ones he has been working on since his first picture. The collaborators are the same — his cinematographer of twenty years, his composer of fifteen — and the result is a film that is both deeply familiar and, in its specifics, freshly painful in a way none of the previous work quite was.

She has been described, irritatingly, as a maker of slow films, and the description has hardened into a brand that does not really fit the work. What the films are is patient, which is a different thing. The new picture is patient in service of a specific argument about the texture of an ordinary marriage, and the patience is what the argument is made of. Calling it slow is to mistake the camera's stillness for the film's metabolism, which is, in fact, ferocious.

The director's first film in five years arrives with the burden of being his return, and the picture is, accordingly, a little too aware of its own arrival. There are several sequences that feel staged for the trailer, several others that feel composed to be quoted in essays about him, and a couple that simply work as scenes in a film. The latter are the best material here, and they are enough to suggest that the next picture, if there is one, may shed the self-consciousness and arrive properly.

Watching the recently restored print, you understand again why this 1974 picture has aged better than nearly any of its contemporaries. The studio-system polish has been replaced, scene by scene, with something rougher and more truthful — a courtyard rendered in actual sunlight, performers permitted to mumble and overlap, a screenplay that resists the closing reassurance the era's audiences had been taught to expect. It is the kind of film that argued, at the time, that the medium could grow up. Half a century on, it still does.

The 1971 thriller arrives on the rep-house circuit looking like a different art form. There are no third-act explanations and no helpful flashbacks. The score is barely there. The lead, in the kind of role that would today be called showy, plays it with the bored exhaustion of a man who already knows how all of this is going to end. The film treats its audience as adults, and the absence of hand-holding feels like an entirely lost form of respect from a cinema we no longer have.

Returning to this picture in middle age, what surprised me is how funny it is. The reputation has hardened into a kind of weighty hindsight reverence, but the 1976 release was, scene by scene, a comedy first. The political darkness is real, but it is the absurdity of meetings and motel rooms and provincial diners that the film actually lives in. Comedy ages badly more often than not, and the laughs in this one have aged extraordinarily well.

The 1977 western, which I had remembered as a slightly minor entry in the director's filmography, is in fact one of his finest. The cinematography uses the desert as character rather than backdrop, and the lead performance is the kind of underplayed work that gives lesser actors permission to do less in similar parts ever after. The film is also notable for refusing to romanticise its violence, a discipline that would be largely abandoned within five years of its release.

Half the appeal of this 1973 picture is the way it lets its actors disappear into a city. The location shooting is doing a tremendous amount of unobtrusive work — the diners are real diners, the apartment buildings are real apartment buildings, the cars on the streets are not extras but actual traffic. The protagonist's slow disintegration takes place inside this fabric and is the more affecting for it. Modern productions can no longer afford to shoot like this, which is, I think, a great loss.

The recently rediscovered cut of this 1978 picture is fifteen minutes longer than the original theatrical release, and almost all of the restored material is connective tissue rather than dramatic incident. It is, as a result, a better film by exactly the texture those fifteen minutes provide. The pacing of the original was already unfashionably slow; the longer version is slower still, and the picture begins to move in the way that a long evening moves, which is exactly the rhythm the story requires.

The 1975 character study is the kind of film no studio would now greenlight, and watching it is a small civic exercise in remembering what was once possible. There is no inciting incident in the first half hour. There is no resolving climax in the last. The protagonist is allowed to be unsympathetic for the entire running time without redemption. The performances are extraordinary, the screenplay is patient, and the picture treats failure as a fully serious subject rather than a setup for triumph.

Watching this 1979 paranoia picture in the present moment is uncanny. The political vocabulary has aged just enough to feel like another country, but the institutional textures — the surveillance hum, the casual bureaucratic obstruction, the hollow press conferences — feel almost contemporary. The lead's slow recognition that the system is not malfunctioning but functioning exactly as designed is the film's central idea, and it remains an unusually mature one for a thriller of any era.

The 1972 picture about a road trip down the Pacific coast is the most relaxed film in the director's career, and possibly his best. There is almost no plot. The performances feel improvised even when they are not. The score is a handful of period songs heard half-muffled through car windows. By the end of the picture, you feel as if you have travelled with these characters for a week, and you are sorry to see them get out of the car. It is a small miracle of a film.

The conventional reading of this 1970 debut — that it is technically rough and morally ambitious — has hardened into something close to received wisdom, and the new restoration is worth seeing precisely because it pushes back against that reading. The picture is, in fact, technically more accomplished than its reputation suggests. The hand-held camera work is purposive rather than accidental. The framing of the long courtroom scene is the work of a confident filmmaker, not a fledgling. The picture has been undersold by its own legend for fifty years.

The film is hand-drawn at a level of detail that current studio economics should no longer make possible, and watching it you understand, scene by scene, where the budget actually went. A character's coat fluttering in a passing breeze contains the gestural information of a small performance in itself. The story is the studio's standard coming-of-age, more sweet than original, but the picture is a sustained argument for what the medium can still do when its makers refuse to compromise on the line.

The new feature from the studio that defined a generation of family animation is the most cynical thing they have ever produced. The character designs are recycled from three previous films, the score is the same composer doing roughly the same job, and the screenplay is the kind of safe inter-generational reassurance that nobody actually needs to be told. There are flashes of the old craft in the backgrounds. The hearts of the people in the foregrounds have, for this one, been allowed to clock off early.

The film's central sequence — a forty-minute traversal of a mountain village in a single autumn afternoon — is one of the most beautiful pieces of animated filmmaking I have seen in years. The light shifts believably as the day moves. The villagers, none of them named, go about their work and contribute incidentally to the story. There is no dialogue at all for the middle twenty minutes, and yet the picture is more emotionally engaged in that silence than most live-action films are at full volume.

The studio's English-language dub is unusually thoughtful, but the picture is still best seen with subtitles. The original voice cast is doing work the localisation cannot quite match, particularly in the small register-shifts that signal hierarchy and politeness in the source language. The animation is luminous in either version. It is the script that loses something in translation, and a great deal of what is being negotiated between the characters lives in the very turns of phrase the dub has to flatten out.

Stop-motion at its current technical peak, this picture is also, more importantly, alive at the level of its handmade textures. The fingerprints on the clay are visible in close-up. The seams of the costumes are intentional. The slight wobble in a character's gait, when it occurs, is the kind of imperfection only this medium can produce. The story is a fairy tale of the older, darker kind, and the director's commitment to handmade craft matches the commitment to handmade cruelty in the source material.

The film attempts something rare in mainstream animation: a story whose central conflict is internal rather than external. The protagonist's adversary is not a villain but a habit of thought, and the picture is structured around her gradual recognition of that pattern. The animation finds visual equivalents for the abstraction without ever lapsing into easy symbolism. By the end the picture has accomplished, in a children's animated feature, something many serious adult dramas attempt and fail at.

The CGI feature studios have learned to make these films interchangeable, and this one is interchangeable in all the predicted ways. The lead is voiced by the comedian whose voice the studio is currently leasing. The sidekick is the small mammal whose toy line is currently being tested. The villain is a comically over-elaborate corporate executive. The animation itself is technically excellent and aesthetically void, and the cinema, when I attended on Saturday afternoon, was full of children who appeared to be enjoying themselves anyway.

The film is the kind of melancholy anime feature that has become the international face of the form: small towns, summer evenings, characters separated by impossibly arranged circumstances, and trains arriving at platforms a few seconds too late. There is nothing exactly original in the assembly. There is, however, real craft in the specifics — a particular cicada sound under a particular rooftop scene, a particular shade of late-afternoon light through a particular train window — and the picture earns its sentiment.

Adult animation continues to be a category most studios cannot quite figure out how to market, and this strange, beautiful film will probably suffer for that. It is animated to look like a moving graphic novel, with thick black lines and watercolour washes, and it tells a story about a divorce that I do not think live action could have rendered as elegantly. The animation is doing something the writing alone could not, which is the only good reason to make an animated film of an adult subject.

The animated documentary, an awkward category, finds in this picture one of its strongest examples. The subject is a Cold War defector whose story can no longer be verified in primary archives, and the director has elected to render the disputed sequences in drawn animation rather than dramatised reconstruction. The decision is morally serious and visually striking. The film never pretends to be showing us the past; it is showing us what the past sounds like in the testimony of a man who is no longer sure of his own memory.

The picture arrived from Cannes carrying the kind of advance reputation that usually punishes a film when it finally screens for the rest of us. In this case the praise is largely deserved. The director's confidence is visible in every shot, the central performance is the most impressive of the year so far, and the structural risk of the second act — a sudden shift in narrator — pays off with a force that the cooler festival coverage did not quite capture. It will divide audiences. It will deserve to.

Festival catnip in the worst sense. The film checks every box the international competition slate currently rewards — austerity of style, marginalised protagonist, ambiguous ending, running time over two hours — and yet the assembly never adds up to a film with a felt centre. The director has clearly read the rubric. The picture is the answer to the question of how to win prizes, not the question of what a story is. By the second hour I was admiring the strategy and feeling nothing.

The festival's late-night sidebar continues to be the more interesting strand, and this entry — a chamber piece set in a single rural petrol station over the course of one rainy night — is the highlight of the section. The two leads are unknowns from the country's small theatre circuit, and they bring a register that no festival regular could have provided. The picture is small in every direction except the one that matters, which is what it asks the audience to feel.

The jury prize seems to have been given to the wrong film in this competition, but that is no new story. The picture that should have been honoured is a quiet, formally precise study of a rural inheritance dispute, made by a director on her second feature. Instead the prize went to a polished international co-production that everyone in the press tent had already decided was the safe choice. The smaller film will find its audience. The prize will, as usual, mostly accrue to the marketing department of the larger one.

The reception at the festival was unusually fractious, and on a second viewing I begin to understand why. The picture is the kind of polemic that mistakes provocation for argument, and reasonable viewers were always going to disagree about whether the film's bad-faith readings of its own characters were an intentional rhetorical move or a structural failure of empathy. I find myself more on the latter side than I did watching it the first time, when the surface tension of the picture briefly carried me.

The new picture from the Iranian director who has been working in exile for the last decade is, as expected, smuggled into being and as a consequence somewhat irregular in technical assembly. The picture is luminous anyway. Shot largely in apartments and at night, on equipment that clearly had to be portable, it accomplishes a moral seriousness that most lavishly resourced festival pictures cannot match. The film is a quiet rebuke to the comforts of how movies usually get made.

The opening film of the festival is rarely the best film of the festival, and this year is no exception. The picture chosen for the slot is a handsome, mostly inert period drama whose virtues are entirely on the surface. The actual interesting work is buried in the third tier of the programme, in a documentary about a Lithuanian collective and a Vietnamese animated feature that almost nobody will see. I would urge readers to seek out the latter when it is released, if it ever is.

What the new South Korean feature understands, and the contemporary American indie scene increasingly does not, is that a screenplay is a structural object and not simply a collection of well-observed scenes. The picture is built like a clock. Every element introduced in the first hour returns, recombined, in the second. The result is the kind of cumulative satisfaction that festival audiences this year have been understandably starved of, and the standing ovation it received at its public screening was, for once, deserved.

The first feature from a Mexican director everyone will be hearing more from. The picture is set across a single dustbowl summer in a small ranching town, and the cinematography has the kind of bone-dry beauty you sometimes get from the dry margins of country-and-western photography. The performances, drawn largely from the local non-professional community, are uniformly excellent. The film is small. The world it suggests is enormous, and one suspects the next picture will move out into it.

The picture is the kind of festival closer that exists to send the audience out into the evening feeling good, and on that limited brief it succeeds. A warm, generous, slightly sentimental comedy-drama, professionally assembled, given a small final emotional kick that does not quite earn its weight but lands anyway because the audience is, by then, primed to be moved. I will probably have forgotten most of it by next weekend. I was glad of it at the time.

There is a peculiar honesty about a film that knows exactly how silly it is and films itself in the long shadow of that fact. The new entry in the killer-shark-but-also-ghost subgenre is one such picture, and the practical effects team have built a marvellous puppet that wobbles in the right ways. The actors, several of whom I last saw doing better work in much smaller films, are clearly enjoying themselves. The picture is bad in all the ways a B-movie is supposed to be bad, which is to say it is good.

The new entry in the absurdly long mutant-rabbit franchise is being released on premium streaming this week, and it is exactly as enjoyable as the previous six. The plot involves a corporate genetics laboratory, a small town with one diner, and a sheriff with a backstory. The kills are inventive, the mutant suit has been redesigned and is now somehow more endearing, and the picture clocks in at a brisk eighty-six minutes. There is more competent craft on display here than in many films four times its budget.

The film has acquired a cult reputation almost entirely on the strength of one sequence — a fight in a roadside motel involving a chainsaw, a fire extinguisher and a startled raccoon — and the rest of it is not quite up to the legend. The performances are flat, the lighting is dim in a way that is mostly not artistic, and the pacing wobbles in the middle act. The motel sequence, however, is genuinely deranged in a way I cannot in good conscience disrecommend.

Watched in the right frame of mind, with the right number of friends in the room, the new straight-to-streaming creature feature is a delight. The CGI is plainly cheap, the screenplay was written in what must have been a single afternoon, and the lead is doing the kind of work that suggests she would rather have been somewhere else. None of this matters. The film has a confident sense of its own pleasures, and within the small territory of those pleasures, it is funny and brisk and oddly satisfying.

A film entirely composed of moments that should not work — the practical-effects helicopter that is obviously a model, the gore that exceeds any reasonable amount of viable blood for a single human body, the romantic subplot between two characters who have spoken three sentences to each other — and that, by some mysterious chemistry, almost entirely does. Cult cinema lives in these gaps between what filmmakers can afford and what they decide to attempt, and this picture sits comfortably in the better half of that tradition.

The new restoration of this 1982 video-store cult favourite reveals a picture rather more thoughtfully made than its reputation suggested. The trim, eighty-minute runtime is the result of obvious cuts but also of unusually disciplined editing, and the kills are staged with a level of geographic clarity that more recent slashers have largely abandoned. The film was made for almost no money and looks it, but the craft within those constraints is real, and the restoration is a small act of cinematic justice.

The film has the unmistakable texture of a project that was begun as one thing and quietly became another partway through production. There are scenes that belong to a much sweeter comedy, scenes that belong to an aggressive horror film, and a final fifteen minutes that suggest somebody, somewhere in post, decided the picture needed to become an action movie. The result is incoherent, occasionally exhilarating, and unlike anything else I have seen this year, which is a sufficient recommendation by my lights.

The new midnight-movie release exists primarily to be watched at midnight by an audience that is partly drunk and entirely committed. It will play badly in any other setting. Within its setting, it is perfectly judged. The dialogue is engineered for the room to shout back at. The set pieces are arranged at the intervals at which a midnight audience would start to lose attention. The picture is not so much a film as a small social occasion, and judged as such it is one of the year's successes.

The trouble with deliberately bad cinema is that the deliberate part tends to leak through, and there is something faintly embarrassing about a film that has been engineered to be enjoyed ironically. This one mostly avoids the trap. The director appears to genuinely love the genre he is working in, and even his most ridiculous flourishes are offered without a wink. The film is bad in the way films are bad when their makers cared too much rather than too little, which is the better kind of bad to be.

I cannot in good conscience call this picture a good film and I would also cheerfully watch it again. The creature suit is magnificent. The screenplay is, in places, unintentionally hilarious. The lead is doing the kind of work that should disqualify a performer from serious roles and which has, on the contrary, only enhanced his cult standing. The picture's principal flaw is that it ends, and I suspect that is the most generous thing one can say about a B-movie in this year of cinema.

The trial occupies the middle two hours of the film and is the most engrossing courtroom drama in a generation. The director resists the temptation to cut away to flashbacks and instead trusts that the testimony itself — careful, slow, contradictory — will be the dramatic material. The judge is played with magnificent neutrality. The witnesses come and go with the unforced texture of real witnesses. By the time the verdict arrives, we have lived through the trial alongside the jury, and the verdict is unbearable in exactly the right way.

The picture is a competent legal procedural that occasionally rises to something more. The procedural beats are reliable. The supporting cast is solid. What lifts it above its category is a single courtroom scene about two-thirds in, in which the defence lawyer, played with extraordinary unfussiness by an actor I had previously dismissed, refuses to cross-examine a witness. The refusal is dramatised at length. The rest of the film never quite reaches that altitude again, but a single moment of genuine craft is enough to recommend the picture.

The court is the closing argument of the genre. Both the prosecution and the defence are doing variants of the same speech we have heard delivered, with the same camera angles, since the 1950s. There is a rule somewhere in this kind of film that you cannot resolve a major dramatic question except via a soaring monologue, and this picture obeys the rule. The monologue is competently delivered. I have, however, run out of patience for the form.

The film centres on a public-defender's tribunal appearance that turns, halfway through, into the most engrossing professional collapse I have seen on film since the seventies. The actress in the central role does extraordinary, almost archeological work, peeling back layer after layer of professional polish until what is left at the lectern is recognisable but not yet broken. The screenplay refuses to forgive her at the end, which is the only honest choice. I will be thinking about this performance for a long time.

Most courtroom films are about the trial. This one is about the discovery period. We spend most of the running time in offices and small windowless conference rooms watching junior associates assemble exhibits, and the picture is unexpectedly gripping. The director has understood that the dramatic mechanics of preparation are at least as compelling as those of performance, and a quietly bureaucratic film about who collects which document and when is, in her hands, a small revelation.

The picture is a courtroom film without a verdict, which sounds a stranger achievement than it turns out to be on screen. The trial collapses in the third act, the case never reaches the jury, and the protagonist must reckon with the kind of partial result that the genre's tidy structure usually denies him. The film is the better for that ambiguity. Audiences raised on a thousand episodes of legal drama may find themselves disoriented; viewers willing to sit with the open ending will find something genuinely thoughtful.

The screenplay is from a former prosecutor, and you can feel that on screen at every level. The procedural details are correct in a way that legal dramas rarely bother to get correct, the small dynamics of objection and ruling have the rhythm of real proceedings, and the way the witnesses look as they enter the room is, for once, accurate. The film is so steeped in the actual texture of practice that the dramatic engine is doing less work than usual, which I count as a virtue.

There is a sequence at the centre of this picture, in chambers with the judge, that may be the best three minutes of legal drama in the last decade. The two senior counsel and the bench find themselves in an off-the-record conversation about how a difficult ruling will be presented, and the picture, normally so committed to the public theatre of the courtroom, allows itself a sudden glimpse of the private craft beneath it. The film never quite recovers its energy afterwards, but that one scene justifies its existence.

The film attempts to render an international tribunal with the kind of intimate dramatic charge that the form usually denies them, and on this it largely succeeds. The translators in the booths get their own subplot. The clerks become characters. The actual proceedings are filmed with the patience required to show the slow accumulation of meaning across days of testimony. It is a more ambitious courtroom film than its mid-range release indicates, and I suspect it will gather a devoted audience in retrospect.

The young public defender is the heart of the picture, and the actress in the role gives a performance of the kind that the genre rarely allows its female leads to give. She is not allowed to be saintly. She is allowed to be tired, sharp-edged, and occasionally wrong. The film loves her without sanctifying her, which is harder to achieve in this category than it should be, and the picture's restraint about her flaws is the most honest political statement it makes.

The film commits to its mockumentary conceit with such patience that it occasionally forgets to be funny, and the picture is the better for it. The fake interviews accumulate weight rather than gags, the talking heads contradict each other in believable ways, and the central pseudo-investigation has the texture of a real local-news story rather than a comedy bit.
