The laughs, when they arrive, arrive almost as a release, and the picture's deepest pleasure is how seriously it takes its own nonsense.

The mockumentary form has been so thoroughly worked over by television that a feature-length entry now has to do something distinctive, and this picture barely tries. The handheld camera, the awkward pauses, the talking-to-camera asides — all of these are deployed exactly as they have been in a thousand previous productions, and the laughs largely depend on the audience recognising the form rather than discovering anything new. The cast is talented. The script is tired. The combination is a passable evening, no more.

The fictional band at the centre of this film is so completely realised that the picture occasionally functions as a music documentary rather than a comedy. The songs, written for the production, are not bad-on-purpose; they are bad-but-believable, which is the much harder register to nail. The band members' interviews are full of the specific micro-grievances real bands have, and the picture's affection for the form is so unstinting that, by the closing credits, I wished the band were real and would be playing somewhere nearby on Saturday.

The film follows a fictional regional planning committee through a season of internal disputes about the relocation of a small roundabout, and against any reasonable expectation the picture is genuinely funny for the full ninety minutes. The cast is uniformly excellent, and the screenplay's affection for the precise institutional language of local government is the rarest of comic gifts. The picture knows the difference between a motion and a resolution, and the difference, in the right hands, turns out to be a comic engine.

The fake documentary about the fake celebrity is, of course, also a satire of real documentary-making about real celebrities, and at its best the picture is operating on both levels at once. The interview-shot lighting is correctly bad. The archival footage is correctly grainy. The talking-head subjects are correctly self-aggrandising. The picture is so committed to the form's habits that the underlying joke about how these documentaries are made is, by the end, sharper than any of the celebrity-focused gags.

The picture's first half is one of the most sustained comic performances of the year. The fictional management consultant at its centre is so precisely observed — the half-coherent jargon, the conference-circuit anecdotes, the watch worn slightly too loosely — that I had to keep reminding myself this was not a real person. The second half loses some of its discipline as the screenplay reaches for an emotional arc the form does not quite support, but the first half alone is worth seeing.

The fake nature documentary about an entirely invented species of burrowing nocturnal mammal is a small triumph of design and performance. The narrator's voice is calibrated almost exactly to the register of every legitimate wildlife documentary I have ever watched. The supposed behavioural footage, generated by some combination of patient practical animation and very careful CGI, is convincing in the way of a magic trick. The film is silly in the best way, which is to say silly and rigorous at the same time.

What the picture understands is that the funniest thing about a real documentary is rarely what the subject says but how they say it, and the imitation of that rhythm is where the comedy lives. The fictional retired conductor at the centre of this film delivers his anecdotes in exactly the cadence of a man who has been telling these stories at dinner parties for forty years. The picture's comedy is at the level of breath, not punchline, and is the better for it.

The film is the rare mockumentary that actually has a point, and the point is sharper than the form usually allows. The fictional reality-television production company at the centre of the picture is a comic creation, but the satire about the labour conditions of its junior producers is real, and the picture earns the right to ask its audience to laugh because it has also done the harder work of asking them to be uncomfortable. It is a smarter film than its premise suggested.

The picture's commitment to its conceit is admirable for the first hour and exhausting for the second. The fake-documentary apparatus, once you have noticed it, becomes its own subject, and the picture has no way to escape the format it has so thoroughly committed to. There are dramatic moments that simply cannot be reached in this form, and watching the screenplay strain towards them is the film's principal frustration. The conceit was a cage. It was, eventually, the wrong cage to put this story in.

The planning sequences of this picture are some of the most pleasurable cinema of the year. The director understands that a heist's principal narrative engine is the explanation of itself, and she spends the first hour giving us a full geometric understanding of the building, the security, and the seven characters' individual capabilities. By the time the heist itself begins, the audience knows enough to anticipate the failures, and the film's pleasures consist almost entirely of those anticipations being broken and reformed in real time.

The new caper is the cinematic equivalent of comfort food, and the cinema I saw it in was, accordingly, perfectly relaxed. The crew is the standard set — the safecracker, the talker, the driver, the inside person — and the screenplay never seriously surprises you. What it does is execute the familiar shapes with such competence and warmth that the absence of surprise becomes the point. Sometimes a film just wants to be the film you expected, and this one wants to be that more than most.

The trouble with the heist genre at the moment is that the screenplays have started to mistake complication for plotting. This picture is a case study. There are seven separate twists, four interlocking double-crosses, and at least two extra plans concealed beneath the surface plan, and the cumulative effect is exhausting rather than thrilling. The actors are doing their best to keep up. The audience, somewhere around the fifth reveal, simply gives up trying to track what was a misdirection in the first place.

What lifts this heist picture above its peers is its interest in what happens on the wrong side of the wall. The screenplay devotes nearly as much time to the security supervisor on the night shift as it does to the crew breaking in, and the picture's central tension is between two skilled professionals who never meet but are reacting to each other's decisions in real time. It is a structural elegance the genre does not often attempt, and the film is the more interesting for the attempt.

The film's central set piece — a forty-minute extended sequence inside the vault complex — is staged with such procedural clarity that it functions almost as a piece of silent cinema. There is virtually no dialogue, the score is replaced by the ambient sounds of the building, and the audience is given the geographic information it needs to follow every action in space. It is the best caper sequence since the heist film's last great revival, and it is worth the ticket on its own.

The picture finally locates a fresh angle on a tired form by setting the heist inside an organisation the crew themselves work for. The protagonist's quiet moral negotiation — robbing the firm he has spent twenty years inside — is the dramatic centre, and the screenplay treats the heist itself almost as the side issue. The film is unfashionably interested in the consequences. The third-act audit-and-investigation material, which most heist films skip entirely, is here the strongest of the film.

An entire heist film built around the planning rather than the execution sounds, on paper, like an exercise. In practice the picture is genuinely thrilling, and the climactic execution sequence is over within ten minutes, almost as a coda. The actors at the planning table are uniformly excellent. The script is precise. The film trusts that the audience would rather watch intelligent professionals work through a problem than watch incompetent ones flail, and the trust is rewarded by some of the year's most concentrated screen time.

The screenplay is doing a great deal of work to disguise the fact that it has no real character beneath the leader of the crew. Every other crew member is rendered through a single trait — the explosives one, the impulsive one, the woman who knew the inside person — and the picture lives or dies by whether the lead can carry the emotional weight of the group. He cannot quite. The actor is doing fine work, but the writing has handed him a chassis rather than a character, and the chassis is showing through.

The film's gimmick — the heist takes place in real time, in a single ninety-minute shot, with no edits — is the kind of thing that should call attention to itself in a damaging way and somehow does not. The choreography of crew, security, cameras and incident is so precisely engineered that the single-take quality reads as urgency rather than virtuosity. The picture is a small miracle of preparation, and I suspect it will be studied by other filmmakers for a long time.

The post-heist material is where this picture finally locates its real subject. The crew has succeeded. The money is in the bag. And then the film follows them, slowly, through six months of waiting in safehouses, growing apart, becoming suspicious of one another, and discovering that the success they had been working towards has not arrived in the form they expected. The picture is finally a film about the impossibility of going home after a victory, and it is the smarter for taking the long route to that question.

The picture is set across a single summer in a coastal town and it has the rare gift of treating its teenagers as actual people rather than vehicles for nostalgia. The screenplay refuses to be sentimental about the period the filmmaker is plainly remembering. The friendships are awkward, the romance is partial, the older relatives are neither saintly nor monstrous, and the ending is small and quiet in the way real summers actually end. It is one of the year's most affecting films.

Another coming-of-age picture about a sensitive boy and his slightly older female friend. The casting is good, the period detail is fine, and the protagonist's narration is just self-aware enough to be irritating without being self-aware enough to step out of the trope it is occupying. The film does nothing actively wrong, which is itself the problem — there is no reason for this picture to exist that I could deduce from watching it, and the genre has had quite enough of its kind recently.

The film centres on a sixteen-year-old taking her first long bus journey alone, and the picture's small accumulated observations about that journey are extraordinary. The actors who play the strangers she meets along the way are uniformly excellent in roles that get five minutes of screen time apiece. The lead, in her debut, has the gift of doing almost nothing convincingly, which is the hardest thing a young actor can be asked to do, and the camera trusts her.

The picture's interest in adolescence is unusually free of nostalgia. The lead is allowed to be embarrassing, irritable, often quite stupid, and only intermittently appealing, which is exactly how adolescents behave in real life. The screenplay refuses to dignify her every choice with a structural payoff. She makes bad decisions and they remain bad decisions. By the end she has not learned a tidy lesson; she has merely become a slightly different person, which is what growing up actually feels like.

The film about a teenage migration across two countries is the rare coming-of-age picture that does not allow the political background to function as scenery. The young protagonist's awakening is inseparable from the geopolitical context, and the screenplay refuses to lift one out of the other for dramatic convenience. The film is intermittently brutal and consistently humane. The actress in the central role is going to win things, and she will deserve to.

There is a particular pleasure in a coming-of-age film that respects its grown-ups. The parents in this picture are not obstacles; they are people, with their own ongoing private failures, and the screenplay allows them to be wrong about specific things and right about others. The teenager at the centre is therefore growing up in a real ecology rather than against a cardboard cutout, and the picture's accumulated emotional weight is the result of that demographic honesty.

The film is a coming-of-age set inside the unusual world of competitive youth chess, and the specificity of the milieu is a real strength. The screenplay assumes you already know how a clock works and does not stop to explain the basic terminology, and the picture is the more respectful for the assumption. The performances at the boards are calibrated to the millimetre. The friendships and rivalries are filmed with the kind of attention to small social texture that most teen films deny themselves.

What is missing from most adolescent films is the boredom, and that is what this picture restores. The long afternoons in which absolutely nothing happens are filmed at the length they actually occupy in a young person's life. The director understands that boredom is not the absence of plot but a particular kind of emotional pressure, and her willingness to film it patiently is what makes the eventual small events feel as enormous as they would feel at that age.

The film is brave enough to end without resolving its central friendship, which is to say with the kind of unfinished business that adolescent friendships usually leave behind in real life. The protagonist returns to school in the autumn. Her friend does not call. The picture refuses the closing reconciliation the audience can feel itself reaching for, and the absence is more affecting than any reconciliation could have been. It is one of the rare coming-of-age films that understands what we actually lose.

Another period coming-of-age picture set in a small town in the 1980s, this one differentiated principally by its willingness to be unhurried. There are entire reels in which almost nothing dramatic happens, and the picture instead trusts that the audience will enjoy spending time in this place with these people. The trust is well placed. The film's accumulated effect is greater than the sum of its scenes, which is the rare achievement, and the closing image is the kind that stays with you on the walk home.

The picture wears its noir inheritance with a knowing shrug, and for once the homage does not curdle into pastiche. The rain is constant, the lighting carves the lead's face into hard planes, and the femme fatale is written with enough interiority that she is finally a person rather than a hazard. What surprised me is how morally exhausted the whole thing feels by the final reel, which is exactly the register the genre's best entries reach for and rarely earn.

Every neon-soaked frame in this crime thriller is doing the work the screenplay refuses to do. The director has plainly studied the look of the genre's modern masters and reproduced it with care, but the plot underneath is a tangle of double-crosses that nobody on screen seems to fully understand. The lead detective broods photogenically through it all. By the time the killer is revealed, I had stopped caring who had done what to whom, and the gorgeous photography only made the indifference sharper.

What lifts this picture above the glut of recent neo-noirs is its willingness to be slow. The investigation unfolds at the pace of an actual investigation, with dead ends that stay dead and witnesses who simply do not know anything useful. The detective is not a genius; he is a tired professional who notices one small thing because he has been doing this for thirty years. The film trusts that procedure, observed honestly, is more gripping than any contrived revelation, and it is right.

The film is set in a coastal city the screenplay never names, and the anonymity is the best decision it makes. The crime at the centre is almost beside the point; what the picture is really tracking is the slow corruption of a decent man who has decided, for reasons the film lets us understand, to look the other way once. The lead gives the performance of his career, and the final scene, played entirely in a parked car, is as quietly devastating as anything in recent crime cinema.

There is a fundamental confusion at the heart of this thriller about whether it wants to be a character study or a puzzle box, and it ends up failing at both. The dialogue keeps reaching for the hard-boiled cadence the genre demands and landing somewhere closer to parody. The plot mechanics are intricate without being satisfying. The cinematography is genuinely beautiful, all wet asphalt and sodium glow, but a film cannot survive on atmosphere alone, and this one tries to for a punishing two hours.

The picture understands something most crime thrillers forget, which is that the most frightening character is rarely the one with the gun. The mid-level fixer at the centre of this film never raises his voice and never threatens anyone directly, and he is, by the final act, the most genuinely menacing screen presence I have encountered in years. The director films his ordinariness as horror. By the closing scene, an ordinary man eating breakfast has become almost unbearable to watch.

A handsome, hollow crime picture that mistakes ambiguity for depth. The screenplay withholds information not because the withholding builds tension but because the writers seem unsure of the answers themselves. The lead investigator is given a tragic backstory delivered in fragments, none of which cohere into a person. The film ends on a freeze-frame that is plainly intended to haunt, and instead simply stops, leaving the audience to assemble a meaning the picture never bothered to provide.

The film's great achievement is its refusal of the redemption arc. The protagonist is a corrupt cop at the start and a corrupt cop at the end, and the screenplay does not flinch from the consequences of that constancy. What changes across the runtime is only how clearly he sees himself, and the picture treats that clarity as its own kind of punishment. It is a bleak, rigorous, beautifully acted film, and I cannot imagine it finding a wide audience, which is the genre's recurring tragedy.

The thriller is structured as a single long night, and the constraint serves it well. The detective moves from one location to the next as the city empties out around her, and the picture accumulates a kind of fatigue that mirrors her own. The dialogue is sharp without being showy. The eventual resolution is smaller than the genre usually permits, a matter of a confession given quietly in a diner at dawn, and the modesty of that ending is precisely what makes it land.

I admired the ambition and resented the execution. The film wants to be a sprawling crime epic in the mode of the genre's great urban tapestries, juggling a dozen characters across a corrupt city, but it has neither the running time nor the screenplay discipline to make the structure cohere. Threads are introduced and abandoned. Characters vanish for forty minutes and return as strangers. There is a genuinely great forty-minute film buried in this overstuffed two-and-a-half-hour one.

The romantic comedy has been pronounced dead so many times that its periodic revivals now feel like resurrections, and this picture is a genuinely lovely one. The two leads have the kind of chemistry that cannot be manufactured in a casting office, and the screenplay is smart enough to keep them apart for the right reasons rather than the contrived ones. The third-act misunderstanding, that ancient curse of the genre, is here resolved with an honesty that made me forgive every previous offender.

Everything about this romantic comedy has been assembled from a kit. The meet-cute happens in a coffee shop, the best friend exists solely to deliver advice, the rival suitor is conspicuously charmless, and the grand gesture takes place at an airport. The two leads are appealing performers stranded in roles that ask nothing of them but to be appealing. The film is not painful to watch, exactly. It is simply the cinematic equivalent of a postcard, pleasant and immediately forgotten.

What this picture grasps, and most of its peers do not, is that the comedy and the romance have to be the same thing. The jokes are not decorations hung on the love story; they emerge from the specific friction between two people who are wrong for each other in interesting ways. The screenplay is dense with the kind of dialogue that rewards attention, and the leads deliver it at the brisk pace the form demands. It is the funniest and the most genuinely romantic film I have seen all year.

The film centres on two people in their sixties, both widowed, both wary, and the decision to age up the genre's central pairing turns out to be its most inspired choice. The obstacles to the romance are not the usual contrivances but the real accumulated weight of two long lives, and the screenplay treats that weight with respect. The picture is funny in a gentle, unhurried register, and it earns an ending that more frantic romantic comedies could never reach.

The picture's fatal flaw is that it does not seem to like either of its lovers very much. The screenplay keeps undercutting them with small humiliations, and the laughs are consistently at their expense rather than alongside them. By the time the film asks us to be moved by their union, we have spent ninety minutes being invited to feel superior to both of them, and the emotional pivot simply does not take. A romantic comedy must, at minimum, want its couple to be happy. This one seems unsure.

There is a long, single-take conversation about forty minutes into this film, conducted entirely while the two leads do the washing up, that is the best scene in any comedy this year. Nothing dramatic happens. They simply talk, and disagree, and circle back, and the rhythm of their disagreement is where the romance quietly takes hold. The director has the confidence to let the scene run, and the trust pays off. The rest of the film is merely good. That scene is something close to perfect.

The screenplay has clearly been worked over by a committee, and the seams show in every scene. There are jokes that belong to a raunchier film and jokes that belong to a sweeter one, and the tonal whiplash never settles. The two leads are doing their professional best, but they have been handed characters whose motivations change between scenes to suit whatever beat the plot requires next. The film is a reminder that the romantic comedy is one of the hardest forms to get right, and that good intentions are not enough.

I went in braced for the worst and came out won over. The premise is hoary, the structure is familiar, and the trailer had given away what looked like every joke. But the picture has a secret weapon, which is a supporting cast given real material instead of the usual disposable comic relief, and the world around the central couple feels genuinely populated. The romance works because it is happening among people we have come to care about, and the film is the rare romantic comedy with a functioning ensemble.

The film is a romantic comedy that has been edited as if it were a thriller, and the mismatch is exhausting. Scenes are cut short before their jokes can breathe, conversations are intercut for a tension the material does not contain, and the score keeps insisting on an urgency the gentle story does not want. Somewhere beneath the frantic assembly is a charming small film about two shy people. The editing has buried it, and I left wishing I could see the director's cut at half the speed.

What I love about this picture is its patience with the unglamorous middle of a relationship. Most romantic comedies end at the first kiss; this one begins there, and spends ninety minutes on the much harder comedy of two people learning to actually live with each other. The jokes come from the negotiation of dishwashers and in-laws and whose friends to see on a Saturday. It is a romantic comedy for adults who have been in relationships, and there are not nearly enough of those.

The sports film is a genre of foregone conclusions, and this picture knows it, which is why it spends so little time on whether the team will win. The actual matches are dispatched briskly. The film's attention is on the locker room, the long bus journeys, the slow erosion of a coach's certainty across a losing season. By treating the sport as the setting rather than the subject, the picture earns an emotional weight the standard underdog narrative never reaches.

Every beat of this boxing picture has been borrowed from a better boxing picture. The training montage arrives on schedule. The wise old trainer dispenses his wisdom. The protagonist loses the first big fight, retreats, rebuilds, and returns for the rematch. The fight choreography is competent and the lead has clearly trained hard, but the screenplay has nothing to offer that the genre has not already said a dozen times, and the film lands with the dull thud of an entirely predictable punch.

The picture follows a women's rowing crew through a single season, and the photography of the sport itself is extraordinary. The director has found camera positions on and around the water that make the physical labour legible in a way I have never quite seen before, the catch and drive of each stroke rendered with real clarity. The drama on land is more conventional, but every time the boat goes back on the river the film locates something close to the sublime, and that is enough.

What this film understands is that the most interesting part of a sporting career is the ending. The protagonist is a footballer two years past his prime, and the picture is a clear-eyed study of a man whose body has begun to refuse the only thing it was ever celebrated for. There is no triumphant final match. There is a quiet, devastating series of smaller defeats, and a performance from the lead that finds the precise texture of an athlete learning to be ordinary.

The film is based on a true story, and it has been crushed flat by its fidelity to the facts. Every scene has the dutiful quality of a screenplay ticking off events that really happened, and the picture never finds the dramatic shape that would have made those events feel inevitable rather than merely chronological. The sport is shot well enough. The people playing it remain strangers. A true story is not the same thing as a story, and this film never closes the gap.

The picture is ostensibly about a marathon runner, but its real subject is obsession, and the director has the courage to make that obsession genuinely unappealing. The protagonist is not a likeable striver; she is a difficult, narrow, frequently cruel person whose single-mindedness costs everyone around her. The film does not soften this, and it does not punish it either. It simply observes, with great precision, the price of being extraordinary at one thing, and the observation is bracing.

There is a genuine pleasure in watching a sports film that respects the intelligence of the sport. This picture, about a chess-like lower-league football manager, assumes the audience can follow a tactical conversation, and it stages its key scenes around whiteboards and substitution decisions rather than last-minute goals. The climactic match is decided not by a wonder strike but by a substitution made in the seventieth minute, and the film has done the work to make that substitution thrilling.

The film commits the cardinal sin of the sports genre, which is to make the actual sport boring. The matches are cut into incoherent fragments, the geography of the field is never established, and the audience is asked to feel the weight of a victory it could not actually follow. The off-field drama is fine. The performances are fine. But a sports film that cannot make its sport exciting has failed at the one task that distinguishes it from every other kind of film.

The picture is a small triumph of focus. It follows a single sprinter through the eighteen months before an Olympic trial, and it refuses every distraction the genre usually reaches for. There is no romantic subplot, no comic-relief teammate, no villainous rival. There is only the training, the injury, the recovery, and the slow recalibration of a life around one event. The discipline of the screenplay mirrors the discipline of its subject, and the film is the better for the symmetry.

I expected another inspirational underdog story and got something stranger and sadder. The film is about a youth basketball coach in a declining mill town, and the games his team plays are almost incidental to the picture's real concern, which is what a sport can and cannot do for a community that the wider economy has abandoned. The film resists the easy uplift. The team's modest success changes very little, and the picture is honest enough to say so, and that honesty is its quiet strength.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The play has been opened up for the screen with such enthusiasm that the thing the stage version did best has been mislaid in the process. On stage, the single confined set was the point; the characters were trapped together, and the audience felt the walls. The film, anxious about cinematic stillness, keeps inventing reasons for the cast to walk outside, and every exterior scene drains a little more pressure from the room. The performances remain superb. The adaptation has misunderstood its source.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: What the director understands, and what most filmed plays do not, is that the camera can be a substitute for the audience's attention rather than a substitute for the stage. She keeps the single apartment setting and films it as a confinement, and the close-ups do the work that a theatre audience's leaning-forward used to do. The result is the rare screen adaptation that is genuinely cinematic without betraying the claustrophobic intimacy that made the play work in the first place.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The film preserves the play's text almost intact, and the text was always the source's great strength, so the picture inherits a real verbal richness. The trouble is the staging, which is so reverent that the camera barely moves for two hours, and the cumulative effect is closer to a recorded performance than a film. The performances are the kind of full-throated theatrical work that plays beautifully from the stalls and lands slightly too large in close-up. It is worth seeing. It is not, quite, a film.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The adaptation makes the bold decision to keep the play's direct addresses to the audience, with the protagonist turning to confide in the camera, and against expectation the device survives the translation intact. On stage the monologues broke the fourth wall; on screen they become something more intimate, a kind of confession to a single listener. The director has found a genuine cinematic equivalent for a theatrical convention, and the film is alive in a way that filmed plays rarely manage to be.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The screenwriter has cut nearly a third of the original text, and every cut is the wrong one. The play's slow accumulation of small revelations has been compressed into a brisk series of confrontations, and the careful rhythm that made the stage version devastating has been lost. The film moves efficiently from plot point to plot point and feels, throughout, like the synopsis of a much better work. The cast deserved the full play. The audience deserved it too.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The single greatest pleasure of this adaptation is watching the original stage cast, all of whom have been retained, perform material they have plainly inhabited for years. There is a lived-in ease to the ensemble work that no newly assembled film cast could replicate. The director has wisely stepped back and let them work, and the camera's principal job is simply to be in the right place to catch the looks that pass between actors who have done this scene three hundred times.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The adaptation has been handsomely mounted, expensively cast, and fundamentally misjudged. The play was a chamber piece, a small bitter argument among four people, and the film treats it as an epic, with sweeping location work and a swelling score. Every cinematic flourish makes the material seem smaller rather than larger, because the flourishes keep insisting on a grandeur the writing was never reaching for. A modest film of a modest play would have been a triumph. This is a bloated film of a modest play.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The film keeps the play's real-time structure, ninety minutes of story told across ninety minutes of screen time, and the constraint gives the picture a relentless forward pressure. The director has resisted the urge to fragment the timeline, and the audience experiences the central confrontation at exactly the pace the characters do. It is an unfashionable kind of filmmaking, patient and confined, and it is also, by the final scene, almost unbearably tense. The stage origins are an asset, not a limitation.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: There is a peculiar flatness to this adaptation that took me a while to diagnose. The performances are good, the text is intact, the direction is competent. What is missing is the live audience, and the play, it turns out, was written to be completed by that audience's presence. The long pauses that drew a held breath from a theatre crowd simply sit there on screen. Some plays survive the transfer to film. This one needed the room, and the room could not be transferred.

subtopic: screen adaptation of a stage play
sentence: The director has done the unthinkable and improved on a celebrated play, largely by trusting the camera to find what the stage could only gesture at. The pivotal scene, which on stage relied on a character described offstage, is here finally shown, and the showing transforms the meaning of everything around it. Purists will object. They will be wrong. This is what a screen adaptation should be: not a recording of a play but a genuine rethinking of it for a medium that can do different things.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The newly restored print of this 1924 feature is a revelation, and not only for the obvious technical reasons. Freed of the murk that decades of bad prints had imposed, the film's astonishing visual storytelling finally registers. There is a chase sequence across a moving train that is as legible and as thrilling as anything in modern action cinema, accomplished entirely through composition and cutting. We have spent a century underrating this director, and the restoration is a quiet correction.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: Watching this 1919 melodrama with a live orchestral accompaniment, I was struck by how completely the modern viewer has lost the skill of reading a silent performance. The lead actress is doing extraordinarily precise work, an entire emotional architecture built from the angle of a shoulder and the timing of a glance, and it took me a full reel to recalibrate my attention to receive it. The film is not primitive. We have simply become illiterate in its language, and that is our loss, not the film's.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The 1927 epic has been reconstructed from three incomplete prints, and the seams are visible, with image quality lurching between sources and a handful of scenes surviving only as production stills with explanatory titles. None of it matters. What survives is overwhelming. The crowd sequences, mobilising thousands of extras across genuine landscapes, have a physical reality that no digital crowd has ever matched, and the film's central performance remains one of the most committed ever captured.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The picture is one of those early sound-era curiosities, made in the brief window when the cameras had to be locked inside soundproof booths, and the technical constraint has frozen the film into a stiff series of static tableaux. The actors stand in tight clusters around hidden microphones, declaiming. It is a fascinating historical document and a fairly tedious film, and the modern viewer is best served by watching it as evidence of a medium in the middle of forgetting everything it had learned.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: This 1922 comedy is, scene for scene, funnier than nearly anything released this year. The physical invention of the central performer is inexhaustible, each gag built on the last with the precision of an engineer, and the picture's climactic set piece, involving a department store and a runaway lift, is a masterpiece of escalating mechanical comedy. We talk about silent comedy with a certain museum reverence. We should be talking about it as a living standard that modern comedy has mostly failed to meet.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The new score commissioned for this 1916 restoration is, regrettably, the worst thing about the screening. The composer has written a relentlessly busy accompaniment that insists on underlining every moment, and the film's images, which are perfectly capable of speaking for themselves, are smothered. Silent cinema at its best leaves room for the audience's own attention. This score fills every silence, and the picture, paradoxically, becomes harder to hear.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The 1925 picture is a reminder that the silent era's visual experimentation went far beyond anything the sound years would attempt for decades. There is a dream sequence in the second reel, accomplished through multiple exposures and hand-tinting, that is genuinely disorienting in the way the filmmaker plainly intended. The narrative is a slight thing, a melodrama of inheritance and disguise, but the picture's formal daring is undimmed by a hundred years, and it still feels like an experiment in progress.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: I had always been told this 1913 feature was a foundational work of the medium, and I went to the restored screening expecting to admire it dutifully and feel nothing. Instead I was genuinely moved. The film's storytelling is simpler than what would come later, but the simplicity has its own clarity, and the central performance, untrained by any later school of screen acting, has a directness that the more polished work of the following decades would partly lose. It is not a relic. It is a film.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The restoration team has done heroic work on this 1928 picture, one of the last great silent features made just as the form was being abandoned, and the film carries the poignancy of a medium at the height of its powers being discarded. The visual sophistication is total. Every shot is composed with an assurance that the early sound years would not recover for a decade. Watching it, you feel the loss of the films that this tradition would have made if it had been allowed to continue.

subtopic: silent film and early cinema reviews
sentence: The picture is an early trick film, barely twelve minutes long, and it has survived precisely because it was never thought important enough to be worth destroying. Watching it now, the modern viewer can see the entire grammar of cinema being invented in real time, the filmmaker discovering, shot by shot, that a cut can move us through space, that a closer view can direct our attention. It is less a film than a record of a medium teaching itself to think, and it is enthralling.

The film consists of a single fixed shot of a window over the course of a full day, and I will not pretend the first hour was not a test of my patience. But somewhere in the afternoon light a shift occurred, in the film or in me, and the picture's actual subject came into focus, which is the texture of time itself when nothing is permitted to distract from it. By the time the window darkened I felt I had been somewhere, and I cannot quite explain where.

The avant-garde has a long and honourable tradition of difficulty, but difficulty must be earned, and this picture mistakes opacity for rigour. The found footage is assembled without any discernible organising principle, the soundtrack is a wash of unmodulated noise, and the eighty-minute running time feels like a dare rather than a structure. There may be a film here that rewards the kind of attention I was unable to sustain. I suspect there is not, and the picture's defenders are responding to its reputation.

The picture is composed entirely of footage shot on expired film stock, and the chemical decay of the medium becomes the film's actual content. Images bloom and corrode, colours shift toward impossible registers, and the figures within the frames are gradually consumed by the deterioration of the material recording them. It is a film about mortality made by allowing the medium itself to die on screen, and it is one of the most genuinely moving experimental works I have encountered in years.

There is a kind of structural film that builds its meaning from a strict formal system, and this picture announces its system in the first minute and then executes it with relentless discipline for the next seventy. Each shot is exactly four seconds long. Each cut moves one step further along a journey through a single building. The pleasure, and there is real pleasure here, is in watching a rigid constraint generate unexpected emotion, and the film delivers it.

The film projects two separate images side by side for its full duration, and the audience is left to negotiate the relationship between them. Sometimes the panels rhyme. Sometimes they argue. Often they simply coexist, and the eye must choose. It is exhausting in the way that genuine attention is exhausting, and it is also, in its best stretches, revelatory about how completely conventional cinema makes that choice on our behalf. I admired it more than I enjoyed it, which the filmmaker would, I think, accept as the correct response.

This is the kind of avant-garde picture that arrives wrapped in a dense theoretical statement, and the statement is, regrettably, more interesting than the film. The on-screen work is a procession of slow dissolves between abstract textures, accompanied by a drone, and it does not in practice do any of the things the programme notes claim for it. The gap between an experimental film's ambitions and its achievements is a familiar one, and this picture falls squarely into it.

The filmmaker has spent a decade photographing a single stretch of coastline, and the picture compresses those ten years into forty minutes, the same shoreline cycling through seasons and erosions and rebuildings. There is no narration and no human figure. There is only the slow geological argument of land and water, and the cumulative effect is something close to awe. It is experimental cinema at its most patient and least pretentious, a film that simply looks, for a very long time, at one true thing.

The picture is built from thousands of single frames, each held for the briefest possible instant, and the result is a flicker film that operates almost directly on the nervous system. I do not recommend it for anyone with the slightest sensitivity to strobing light. For those who can withstand it, the film induces genuinely strange perceptual states, after-images and phantom colours that the picture is plainly engineering. It is less a film to be watched than a film to be undergone.

What is unexpected about this experimental feature is its warmth. The avant-garde is often a chilly place, more interested in the audience's intellect than its feelings, but this picture, a collage of home-movie footage from a single extended family across sixty years, uses its formal strategies in the service of an enormous tenderness. The fragmentation is not a barrier to feeling; it is the form that memory actually takes, and the film knows it.

The film is silent, black and white, and entirely without recognisable images, a seventy-minute progression of abstract forms generated by exposing the film stock directly to light and chemical. It is, by any conventional measure, nothing at all. And yet sitting with it in a dark room, I found my attention undergoing a slow transformation, settling into a register I rarely reach, and I left convinced that the picture had done something to me even though I cannot name a single thing it showed.

The espionage picture has spent two decades trying to out-explode the action genre, and it is a genuine relief to find one that remembers the form's older pleasures. This film is mostly people talking quietly in offices, and the tension comes from what is not being said across those desks. The protagonist never fires a weapon. The climax is a conversation. And the picture is more genuinely nerve-wracking than any of the recent gadget-laden entries, because it understands that the real currency of spying is trust and its absence.

The film wants very badly to be a sophisticated le Carré-style study of institutional betrayal, and it has the trench coats and the grey European cities to prove it. What it lacks is the patience and the intelligence the model requires. The plot moves too fast to register as labyrinthine and too slow to function as a thriller, and the central mole is identifiable from the first reel by anyone who has seen this kind of film before. It is a handsome imitation of depth.

What this picture grasps about espionage is the loneliness of it. The protagonist is a deep-cover agent who has been living a fabricated life for so long that the fabrication has become the only life she has, and the film is less a thriller than a study of that erosion. The plot, when it intrudes, is almost an irritation. The picture is at its best in the quiet domestic scenes, watching a woman perform a marriage she no longer remembers how to feel, and the performance is shattering.

The action set pieces in this spy thriller are competent and the globe-trotting is glossy, but the film commits the genre's modern cardinal sin, which is to make the espionage itself incomprehensible. Nobody in the audience could explain, after the credits, what the stolen device does, who wanted it, or why it mattered. The picture substitutes momentum for clarity and hopes we will not notice. We notice. A spy film must, at minimum, let us understand what is being spied upon.

The picture is set during a single tense week of a Cold War posting, and the period detail is exact without being fetishistic. The film understands that the great drama of espionage is bureaucratic, that the most consequential scenes happen when one officer decides whether to forward another officer's report, and it stages those small administrative betrayals with the gravity of combat. It is a slow, intelligent, deeply pessimistic film, and it is the best of its kind in a decade.

The film's twist, when it arrives, is so heavily foreshadowed that calling it a twist is generous, and the screenplay's evident pride in the reveal is the most embarrassing thing about the picture. The lead is doing solid work in an underwritten role. The supporting cast of handlers and double agents is interchangeable. The whole production has the air of a genre exercise assembled by people who have seen many spy films and understood none of them, and the result is two hours of glossy nothing.

There is a sequence at the centre of this espionage picture, a dead-drop exchange in a crowded railway station, that is staged with such precise control of information that I held my breath for its entire ten minutes. We know what the agent knows, we know what she does not, and we can see the danger she cannot, and the director orchestrates those gaps with the skill of a master. The rest of the film is merely good. That sequence is a small masterpiece of pure cinema tension.

The picture is unusual among modern spy films in being genuinely interested in the moral cost of the work. The protagonist is good at his job, and the film makes us understand that being good at this particular job means betraying people who trusted him, repeatedly, as a matter of routine professional competence. There is no glamour here. The screenplay treats each betrayal as a small wound to the man's character, and by the final scene the accumulated damage is visible on his face.

The film is a spy thriller with the unusual ambition of being told entirely from the perspective of the analysts, the people who never leave the office and who experience the whole operation as a stream of incomplete intelligence. It is a bold structural choice, and for an hour it works beautifully, generating tension from interpretation rather than action. The final act loses its nerve and cuts to the field, and the picture is the weaker for the betrayal of its own premise.

I have seen a great many spy films in which the tradecraft is decorative, a set of cool-looking behaviours signifying competence, and it is a pleasure to encounter one in which the tradecraft is the drama. This picture takes the time to show why an agent walks a particular route, why a particular café is chosen, what the cost of a single error in routine would be. The audience learns to think like a spy, and once we are thinking that way, the film's quiet crisis becomes genuinely terrifying.

The film has clearly spent its enormous budget on the world rather than the story, and the world is, to be fair, magnificent. The invented landscapes have a geographical coherence that fantasy cinema rarely bothers with, and the creatures feel like the products of an actual ecology. But two and a half hours into this gorgeously rendered place, I realised I did not care whether the prophecy was fulfilled, because the screenplay had given me a hero defined entirely by his destiny and not at all by his character.

What this epic understands is that the scale must serve the intimacy, not replace it. There are vast battles here, and they are well staged, but the film keeps returning to a single friendship between two ordinary people swept up in events too large for them, and it is that friendship the picture asks us to care about. By the time the largest of the battles arrives, we are watching it through the eyes of people we love, and the spectacle finally has a reason to exist.

The fantasy adventure has become a genre of exhausting completeness, every corner of its world explained, every magical rule codified, every culture given its appendix of lore. This picture is a quiet rebellion against that tendency. Its magic is genuinely mysterious, never fully accounted for, and the film is the more enchanting for its restraint. The protagonist does not understand the forces she is moving among, and neither do we, and that shared bewilderment is the source of real wonder.

The picture is the first installment of a planned trilogy, and it shows, in all the ways that phrase has come to dread. The film is structurally a prologue, three hours of setup for stories that have not yet been told, and it ends not with a conclusion but with a promise. The world is richly imagined and the cast is strong, but a film should be a film, and this one is a trailer for two other films, expensively disguised as a complete work.

The adventure is propelled by a quest so familiar that the audience can map its waypoints in advance, and yet the picture keeps finding small surprises in the execution. The wise mentor dies, as wise mentors do, but the film stays with the grief for an unfashionably long time. The dark lord is defeated, as dark lords are, but the victory is treated as a loss as much as a triumph. The shape is ancient. The texture of the telling is fresh enough to redeem it.

The digital effects in this fantasy epic have reached the point of total photorealism, and the picture is, paradoxically, the worse for it. When the dragons were puppets and the armies were extras, the eye registered a physical reality. Now everything is equally weightless and equally possible, and the spectacle no longer means anything because nothing in it could ever have failed. The film is a flawless rendering of events that never, in any sense, happened, and the flawlessness is its central emptiness.

The film adapts a beloved fantasy novel, and the adaptation has been made by people who plainly love the book and have, in their love, forgotten that the audience has not read it. Characters arrive with the assumption that we already know them. Places are named as if their significance is established. The picture is dense with a reverence the uninitiated viewer cannot share, and the result is an epic that will delight its existing fans and bewilder everyone else.

There is a sequence midway through this epic, a long crossing of a frozen mountain pass, that achieves the genuine sublime. The director slows the picture almost to a halt, the score drops to a single sustained note, and the company of travellers becomes small dark figures against an overwhelming white expanse. For a few minutes the film stops being an adventure and becomes a meditation on human smallness, and the rest of the picture, good as it is, never quite reaches that altitude again.

The picture is a fantasy adventure that has decided, refreshingly, to be funny. The quest is genuine and the stakes are real, but the screenplay never loses its sense of the inherent absurdity of prophecies and chosen ones, and the heroes are allowed to be irritated by the inconveniences of destiny. The humour does not undercut the wonder; it grounds it, makes the magic feel like something that happens to actual people. It is the most purely enjoyable fantasy film in years.

The epic runs to nearly three hours, and for the first two of them I was wholly under its spell. The world-building is generous, the performances are committed, and the central journey has a real momentum. Then the film reaches its enormous final battle, and the picture seems to lose all confidence in the human story it had been telling, drowning its characters in an hour of indistinguishable digital carnage. A great film is in here, and it ends, in my estimation, around the two-hour mark.

The picture is built on a single destabilising question, and the director is disciplined enough never to answer it. We are never told whether the protagonist's mounting paranoia is justified or symptomatic, and the film makes us live inside that uncertainty for two hours. It would be an unbearable trick if the lead performance were not so calibrated, holding the line between victim and unreliable narrator without ever tipping the audience off. By the closing scene I trusted nothing, including my own attention, which is exactly where the film wanted me.

Every psychological thriller now seems contractually obliged to deliver a third-act twist, and this one obliges so dutifully that the twist arrives drained of all surprise. The screenplay has spent ninety minutes laying a trail of obvious clues, and the eventual reveal is less a shock than the confirmation of a suspicion the film had practically printed in the programme. The lead is doing genuinely unsettling work. The structure she has been handed undermines her at every turn.

What this film understands is that the most effective psychological horror is domestic. There are no killers and no conspiracies here, only a marriage in which one partner has begun, very gradually, to doubt the other's account of small shared memories. The picture stages this erosion in ordinary rooms over ordinary dinners, and the cumulative dread is more genuine than any thriller with a body count. It is a quiet, exact, deeply disturbing film about the fragility of the agreements we call a life.

The film is so committed to its atmosphere of unease that it forgets to give the unease anywhere to go. For two hours the protagonist drifts through dim apartments and overhears ambiguous conversations, and the picture mistakes this sustained discomfort for tension. But tension requires the possibility of resolution, and this film never offers one, never escalates, never pays anything off. It is a mood piece masquerading as a thriller, and the mood, however well-crafted, is not enough.

The picture's central conceit, that the protagonist may be being slowly manipulated by everyone in her life, is the oldest trick in the psychological-thriller book, and the film knows it, and the knowing is what makes the picture work. The director plays openly with our genre expectations, letting us run ahead of the plot and then quietly demonstrating that our suspicion was itself a kind of manipulation. It is a film about paranoia that makes the audience complicit in the paranoia, and the effect is genuinely vertiginous.

The lead actress is doing the heavy lifting of an entire genre here, and she is more than equal to it. The screenplay asks her to be sympathetic and suspect in the same gesture, to make the audience care for a woman they cannot trust, and she finds a register of frayed warmth that holds both at once. The film around her is competent rather than inspired, but her performance is the kind that drags a middling thriller up into something worth seeing.

The picture takes place almost entirely inside a single character's recovering memory, and the unreliability is structural rather than decorative. Scenes are replayed with small differences, conversations shift their meaning on the second hearing, and the audience is asked to assemble the truth from a set of contradictory drafts. It is a demanding film, and it does not flatter the viewer with a tidy final version of events. The refusal is the point, and it is a brave one in a genre addicted to closure.

There is a fundamental dishonesty to this thriller that soured me on it well before the end. The film withholds a crucial piece of information not from the characters but from the audience alone, and it does so by actively misrepresenting what we are shown. The eventual reveal therefore does not reframe the story; it simply admits that the picture lied to us. A psychological thriller can keep secrets. It cannot cheat, and this one cheats, and the cheating undoes everything that came before.

The film unfolds across a single sleepless night, and the constraint gives it a feverish coherence. The protagonist's grip on reality loosens in real time, and the director synchronises the film's grammar to that loosening, the edits growing more abrupt, the colour palette sliding, the sound design beginning to lie. By dawn we are as exhausted and as uncertain as the character, and the picture's final image, ordinary and quiet, lands with the force of a verdict. It is a small, expertly controlled film.

The picture is intelligent about a great many things and finally undone by its ending. For most of its length it is a genuinely unnerving study of a man who cannot tell whether he is being gaslit or simply losing his grip, and the ambiguity is held with real skill. Then the screenplay panics, and the final ten minutes deliver a brisk, literal explanation that resolves every question the film had so carefully kept open. It is the sound of a film losing faith in itself at the last possible moment.

The film assembles a dozen significant characters and, against all odds, gives each of them a genuine interior life. The screenplay's structural achievement is that no thread feels like filler, no character feels like a device, and the cross-cutting between stories generates meaning rather than mere momentum. The ensemble is uniformly excellent, but the real star is the editing, which knows precisely when to leave one story and which fragment of another to land on. It is a master class in choreographing a crowd.

The trouble with an ensemble piece this large is that the screenplay has roughly nine minutes for each of its many characters, and nine minutes is not enough to build a person. The film introduces a dozen lives, sketches each in a few broad strokes, and then asks us to be moved when their paths cross. We are not moved, because we do not know them, and the picture's busy structure has mistaken the quantity of characters for the richness of a world.

What lifts this ensemble drama is the director's evident trust in her actors. There is a long dinner-party sequence at the centre of the film, with eight people around a table, and she simply lets the camera move among them as the conversation overlaps and fractures and reforms. No single character dominates. The scene is built from a hundred small reactions, and the cumulative effect is the rare sensation of watching a genuine group of people rather than a cast assembled to perform one.

The picture follows the residents of a single apartment building over the course of a difficult year, and the building itself becomes the organising intelligence of the film. Characters pass each other on the stairs, overhear each other through the walls, and slowly, almost without noticing, become consequential to one another. The screenplay never forces the connections. It lets them accrue, and by the final scene the ensemble has become something like a community, which is harder to dramatise than it sounds.

The ensemble film lives or dies by its balance, and this one is fatally unbalanced. Three of the storylines are vivid and well-acted; the other four are thin, and the film keeps dutifully returning to them out of structural obligation rather than dramatic need. Every cut away from the good material to the weak material is felt as a loss. A braver edit would have cut the picture down to the three stories that work, and it would have been a far better film.

The casting director should receive a credit above the title. This ensemble piece works almost entirely because every role, down to the smallest, has been filled by exactly the right face and voice, and the film generates a great deal of its pleasure simply from the rightness of its people. The screenplay is solid without being exceptional. The direction is unobtrusive. But the gathered cast has a collective texture, a sense of having been chosen with real care, and it carries the whole film.

The picture is one of those holiday-gathering ensemble dramas in which an extended family convenes under one roof and the old wounds are reopened over the course of a long weekend. The form is familiar, but the film executes it with unusual honesty. Nobody is redeemed by the closing scene. The reconciliations are partial and provisional, the way real family reconciliations are, and the ensemble is good enough to make every grudge and every grudging truce feel earned.

The film is structured as a relay, each character handing the narrative to the next as their paths intersect across a single city over a single day. It is a clever conceit, and it sustains itself for about an hour before the cleverness begins to feel like a constraint. The handoffs grow contrived, the coincidences strain, and the picture becomes a demonstration of a structural idea rather than a story. The ensemble deserved a looser frame, and the frame slowly suffocates them.

What is unusual about this ensemble picture is its generosity to its minor characters. The film grants its smallest roles, the waiter, the neighbour, the woman behind the desk, a moment of unguarded interiority that does not advance the plot at all. These moments could be cut and the story would survive. But the world would be poorer, and the director plainly understands that an ensemble film is, finally, an argument about how many people deserve our attention. This one argues generously.

The picture brings together a famous cast of a dozen recognisable faces, and the recognisability turns out to be the problem. Every time a beloved actor appears in a small role, the film stops dead for a beat of audience recognition, and the ensemble never quite coheres into a fictional world because it keeps reminding us it is a parade of stars. A genuine ensemble requires a degree of anonymity, a willingness to disappear into the group, and this glittering cast is constitutionally unable to disappear.

It is the rare debut that arrives fully formed, and this one mostly does. The young director has a confident visual sense and an even more impressive sense of restraint, knowing exactly when to hold a shot and when to cut away. There are first-feature wobbles, a slightly overwritten voiceover, a third act that resolves a beat too neatly, but they are the wobbles of genuine talent. This is a filmmaker worth following, and the picture is a real arrival.

The debut feature has all the marks of a filmmaker who has watched a great many films and not yet lived quite enough life to fill one. The picture is dense with stylistic flourishes, every one of them borrowed from a director the newcomer admires, and the borrowed gestures never settle into a voice of their own. There is undeniable craft here. What there is not, yet, is a reason for the film to exist beyond the maker's evident desire to make a film.

What I admired most about this first feature is its modesty. The young director has resisted every temptation to announce herself, every showy camera move and clever transition that a debut so often uses to demand attention. Instead she has made a small, patient, observant film about a single family, and she has trusted the material to register. It is an unfashionable kind of debut, quiet and assured, and it suggests a long career rather than a brief one.

The debut is plainly autobiographical, drawn from the director's own childhood in a particular industrial town, and the specificity is the picture's great strength and its eventual limitation. The detail is exact and the affection is genuine, and for an hour the film is a vivid act of remembering. But memory is not yet structure, and the picture's final third drifts, accumulating incident without shape, as if the director could not bear to leave anything out. The next film, freed of the autobiography, may be the real one.

A first feature of startling formal ambition, and the ambition mostly pays off. The young director has built the picture around an unconventional structure, three timelines braided together without signposting, and a less confident newcomer would have lost control of it within twenty minutes. This one does not. The picture is demanding and occasionally cold, but it is the work of a real intelligence, and the technical assurance on display in a debut is genuinely uncommon.

The debut suffers from the most common affliction of first features, which is the conviction that everything must be in it. The young director has poured a decade of ideas into a single ninety-minute film, and the picture is consequently overstuffed, lurching between tones and themes with the restless energy of someone who fears they may never get to make another. There is enough good material here for three films. Compressed into one, it exhausts rather than impresses.

What is remarkable about this debut is the performance the first-time director has drawn from her lead, a non-professional cast in her first screen role. The newcomer's work is wholly without technique and wholly convincing, and a more experienced director might have polished that rawness into something less true. The young filmmaker had the instinct to leave it alone, and that instinct, the knowing of what not to do, is the surest sign of a real director in a first feature.

The debut arrives carrying a great deal of festival buzz, and the buzz has, as buzz tends to, oversold it. The film is a perfectly respectable first feature, competently made and sincerely felt, and in a quieter year it would attract a quieter and more accurate response. The young director has talent. The picture is promising. But promise is not the same thing as achievement, and the gap between the two has been papered over by a publicity apparatus that needed a discovery this season.

The first-time director has done something genuinely hard, which is to make a small film feel complete. There is no sense, watching this debut, of a filmmaker reaching beyond her means or padding a thin idea to feature length. The story is exactly the size of the running time. The visual style is exactly as elaborate as the material requires and no more. It is the work of someone who already understands the most difficult thing about directing, which is knowing what kind of film you are actually making.

There is a sequence in this debut, a single unbroken shot following the protagonist through a crowded house party, that announces the arrival of a real filmmaker more clearly than any amount of advance press. The choreography of camera and crowd and incident is the work of someone with a genuine spatial imagination. The rest of the film does not always live up to that sequence, but a debut only needs to contain one moment of undeniable command, and this one contains several.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film has a single job, which is to make the viewer at home feel something close to the energy of the room, and this picture fails it almost completely. The editing cuts away from every performance at exactly the moment a musical phrase begins to build, the camera is more interested in the audience than the stage, and the sound mix has flattened a live show into a sterile studio gloss. The band is plainly extraordinary live. You would never know it from this film.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: What this concert film understands is that the camera should serve the music rather than perform alongside it. The director keeps her shots long, lets the songs play out in something close to real time, and trusts that watching a great musician work is interesting enough without constant intervention. The result is the rare concert film that genuinely transports, and by the encore I had forgotten I was watching a screen rather than standing in the crowd.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The music documentary follows a band through the recording of a difficult album, and the picture is at its best in the studio, watching the slow argumentative labour of making something. The talking-head interviews are the standard fare, and the archival material has been seen elsewhere. But the footage of four people in a room disagreeing about a chord progression has a genuine tension, and the film, when it stays in that room, captures something true about collaboration that the rock-documentary genre rarely reaches.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The picture is a hagiography in concert-film clothing. The artist at its centre is presented without a single moment of friction or doubt, the interviews are uniformly adoring, and the film has the suspiciously frictionless texture of a project made with the subject's full cooperation and full editorial control. The performance footage is good. The portrait around it is so flattering as to be useless, and the audience leaves having been sold something rather than shown anything.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film captures a single legendary night, and the director has wisely resisted the temptation to dress it up. There is no narration, no interview material, no context beyond the performance itself. The picture simply presents the show, song by song, from the soundcheck to the final bow, and the absence of editorial intervention is what makes it work. We are given the night, whole, and asked to make of it what we will, and what I made of it was something close to elation.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The music documentary about the forgotten session musician is a small act of restitution, and a genuinely moving one. The subject played on dozens of famous records and was credited on almost none of them, and the film patiently reconstructs a career that the official histories erased. The archival detective work is impressive, but it is the footage of the man himself, now elderly, listening to his own uncredited playing, that gives the picture its quiet devastating force.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The picture is a music documentary that has confused access with insight. The filmmakers were granted extraordinary proximity to the artist, and the screen is full of intimate footage, backstage, on the bus, in hotel rooms. But proximity alone reveals nothing, and the film never finds an angle, a question, an argument about its subject. It simply follows him around for two hours, and at the end we have been very close to a person we have not, in any meaningful sense, come to know.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The concert film is shot across three nights of the same tour, and the director has cut between them with such skill that the seams are invisible, assembling an idealised single performance from the best moments of each. Purists may object to the artifice. I found it exhilarating. The film is not a document of one night but a portrait of what the band was capable of on its best night, and the editing's quiet construction of that ideal is itself a kind of love letter to the music.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: The music documentary covers the genre's familiar rise-and-fall arc, and it covers it competently, and I cannot pretend I needed to see it. The interviews are well-conducted, the archival footage is well-sourced, the narrative is well-shaped. But everything in the film is precisely what the form has trained us to expect, and the picture never once surprises, never finds the strange specific detail that would lift it out of the template. It is a perfectly professional act of telling us what we already knew.

subtopic: concert film and music documentary reviews
sentence: What makes this concert film extraordinary is its attention to the audience. The director keeps returning, between songs, to faces in the crowd, and the picture slowly becomes as much about the act of listening as the act of performing. By the final number, when the camera holds on a single weeping stranger for an uncomfortably long time, the film has made an argument about what music is for, and the argument is more eloquent for never being spoken aloud.

The revisionist western has been revising the same handful of myths for fifty years now, and this picture has nothing fresh to add to the conversation. We get the brutal demystification of frontier violence, the morally compromised lawman, the unromantic mud and disease, and all of it has been done before and done better. The cinematography is genuinely beautiful, all vast skies and small figures. But beauty is not an argument, and the film has no argument the genre has not already exhausted.

What this western understands is that the landscape is the antagonist. The human conflicts in the picture are real enough, but the director keeps pulling back to show the country itself, indifferent and enormous, and the people scratching at its surface seem smaller with every wide shot. By the final scene, the question of who wins the feud has come to feel almost beside the point, because the land will outlast all of them, and the film has made us feel that geological patience in our bones.

The picture is a western told, for once, from the perspective of the people the genre usually relegates to the background, the homesteading family watching the gunfighters pass through their valley. The shootout that a conventional western would centre is here glimpsed from a distance, through a farmhouse window, and the film's real concern is what the violence costs the bystanders. It is a quiet, humane corrective to a century of mythology, and it earns its revisions honestly.

The film is a throwback western that has decided, against all current fashion, to simply believe in the form. There is a clear hero, a clear villain, a town that needs saving, and a final showdown on a dusty street at noon. The picture executes these ancient shapes without irony and without apology, and the conviction is, after so many decades of revisionism, genuinely refreshing. Sometimes the old myths still have power, and this film trusts that power completely.

The western runs to nearly three hours, and the length is the point. The director has made a film about waiting, about the enormous boredom of frontier life punctuated by sudden lethal violence, and she insists on making the audience feel the duration. It is a demanding picture, and not everyone will have the patience for its long becalmed stretches. But when the violence finally arrives, it lands with a force that no briskly paced western could deliver, precisely because we have waited so long for it.

The picture wants to deconstruct the western and ends up merely decorating it. The screenplay gestures at the genre's complicity in the mythology of conquest, has its characters deliver the occasional speech of self-aware critique, and then proceeds to stage exactly the kind of thrilling gun battle the critique was supposedly dismantling. You cannot have it both ways. A film that wants to interrogate the western's pleasures cannot also serve them up undiminished, and this one tries, and the contradiction hollows it out.

There is a long sequence in this western, a cattle drive across a drought-stricken plain, that contains some of the most extraordinary natural-light photography I have seen in years. The director has waited, evidently for weeks, for exactly the right skies, and the patience is visible in every frame. The story the film is telling is a familiar one of revenge and reluctant redemption, but the picture is worth seeing for the landscape work alone, which is the kind of cinema the western was invented to make possible.

The film is a western set in the genre's twilight, the early years of the new century, when the railways and the fences had begun to close the frontier, and the picture is suffused with a sense of an era ending. The aging gunfighter at its centre is a man whose entire skill set has become obsolete, and the film treats his irrelevance with a tenderness that the genre's harder revisions usually withhold. It is an elegy, and a genuinely moving one.

The picture casts the genre's iconography against itself with real intelligence. The lone rider arriving in town is, this time, a figure of menace rather than salvation; the saloon is a place of tedium rather than danger; the climactic duel is botched and ugly and over in a graceless instant. The film knows every convention it is inverting, and the inversions are precise rather than glib. It is the rare revisionist western that has actually thought about what it is revising.

The western has been beautifully photographed and indifferently written, and the imbalance is fatal.
