Every frame is a postcard, the desert rendered in colours of genuine splendour, and yet the people moving through this gorgeous country are stock figures reciting stock lines. The genre can survive a thin plot. It cannot survive characters this hollow, because the western has always been, at its best, a moral form, and a moral form requires people whose choices we can believe in.

The disaster film has a built-in problem, which is that spectacle has no memory, and this picture never solves it. The earthquake sequence is genuinely staggering, a twenty-minute set piece of collapsing infrastructure rendered with terrifying weight, and then the film must spend ninety minutes following survivors I have no reason to care about. The screenplay has assumed the catastrophe would do the emotional work. It cannot. A disaster film still needs people, and this one forgot to write any.

What this survival picture understands is that the real drama begins after the disaster, not during it. The shipwreck is dispatched in the first ten minutes. The remaining ninety are spent on a raft, and the film has the courage to make those ninety minutes about the slow administrative horror of rationing, the small cruelties of exhaustion, the way a group of strangers negotiates who will be allowed to die first. It is a harrowing, intelligent film about the logistics of catastrophe.

The film strands a single climber on a single mountain for its entire running time, and the constraint is the picture's making. There is almost no dialogue, because there is no one to talk to, and the drama is constructed entirely from the protagonist's diminishing options and the indifferent physics of cold and altitude. The lead carries the film alone, and she is more than equal to the task. It is a survival picture of genuine purity, a problem and a person and nothing else.

The picture is the kind of all-star disaster movie the genre produced in bulk decades ago, and the revival is not as fun as the filmmakers plainly hoped. The famous faces are introduced in their familiar archetypes, the catastrophe arrives on schedule, and the audience settles in to guess the order of the deaths. The effects are expensive and the pace is brisk, but the film never finds the cheerful self-awareness that made the genre's classics enjoyable. It takes its own silliness far too seriously.

The survival film is based on a true story, and for once the fidelity to fact is a strength rather than a straitjacket. The real events were strange enough that no screenwriter would have dared invent them, and the picture wisely resists the urge to dramatise. It simply follows what happened, hour by hour, with a procedural patience that builds an almost unbearable tension. By the rescue, I had been holding my breath, on and off, for an hour, and the relief was physical.

The disaster picture spends so long on the science of its impending catastrophe that the film forgets to be a film. There are lengthy scenes of experts pointing at screens, explaining the mechanics of the coming flood to one another and, transparently, to us. The screenplay has mistaken exposition for tension. When the flood finally arrives, it is almost a relief, not because the spectacle is thrilling but because the lecturing has finally stopped.

What lifts this survival film above its peers is its refusal of heroism. The protagonist does not outsmart the wilderness or conquer the elements. He simply endures, badly, making one poor decision after another, surviving largely by luck, and the film treats this honestly rather than reshaping him into an action hero. It is a humbling picture about the limits of human competence against an indifferent natural world, and the humility is bracing.

The film commits the disaster genre's gravest sin, which is to make the catastrophe boring. The collapsing dam, the spreading wildfire, the sinking liner, all of it is rendered in the same weightless digital register, and after the third enormous spectacle the eye simply stops registering scale. There is a law of diminishing returns in this genre, and the picture, by piling disaster upon disaster, runs straight past it, until the end of the world has become merely tedious.

The survival picture is set in the aftermath of a storm that has cut off a small coastal town, and the film is unexpectedly interested in community rather than individual heroism. The drama is about how a few hundred isolated people organise themselves, share what they have, and decide what they owe one another. It is a quiet, generous film about the social texture of catastrophe, and it suggests that the most important survival skill is not strength but the capacity to cooperate.

There is a sequence in this disaster film, a slow flooding of a subway carriage, that is staged with such claustrophobic precision that I found it genuinely difficult to watch. The director understands that real terror is small and specific, the water at the ankles, then the knees, then the chest, the geometry of the carriage becoming a trap in real time. The rest of the picture is conventional spectacle. That one sequence is a small masterpiece of escalating dread.

The remake exists for no reason that the film itself can articulate. It reproduces the original's plot beat for beat, updates the technology, recasts the roles with current stars, and adds nothing, asks nothing, discovers nothing. The original was not a flawed film waiting to be improved; it was a complete one. This new version is a competent photocopy, and watching it I felt the particular melancholy of seeing something I loved repeated by people who did not understand why it had worked.

What this remake gets right is that it has a genuine reason to exist. The original was a product of its moment, and its central premise has acquired, in the decades since, a wholly new set of resonances. The new film does not simply update the story; it re-thinks what the story now means, and the result is a picture in genuine dialogue with its source rather than merely indebted to it. It is the rare remake that justifies itself.

The reboot has been engineered with the cold precision of a corporate relaunch. Every element of the beloved franchise has been polished, modernised, and made safe, and the resulting film has the texture of a product rather than a story. The new cast is attractive and capable. The effects are state of the art. And the whole enterprise is suffused with a focus-grouped caution that the scrappy original would not have recognised, because the original was made by people taking a risk, and this is made by people protecting an asset.

The remake of a foreign-language original commits the usual crime of the form, which is to sand away every specific cultural texture that made the source distinctive. The story has been relocated, the names have been changed, the strangeness has been smoothed into a generic familiarity, and what remains is a plot stripped of the context that gave it meaning. The original was about a particular place. The remake is about nowhere, and a film about nowhere is, finally, about nothing.

The reboot makes the smart decision to keep its connection to the original loose, taking the premise as a starting point rather than a template, and the freedom serves it well. The new film tells its own story, finds its own tone, and trusts the audience to appreciate the franchise without needing it slavishly reproduced. It will disappoint the purists who wanted a faithful echo. It will reward everyone else, because it is, against the odds, a genuinely good film in its own right.

The remake is so anxious about its predecessor that it cannot stop referencing it. Every few minutes the new film pauses to recreate an iconic shot, quote a famous line, or wink at a beloved moment, and the cumulative effect is a picture that exists in a state of permanent nostalgic deference. A remake must, at some point, become its own film. This one never does. It spends its entire running time bowing to the original, and a film made of bows is not a film at all.

What the reboot understands is that a long-dormant franchise needs new blood, not embalming. The film hands the story to a director with a genuine vision and the freedom to pursue it, and the result is a picture that feels alive in a way the increasingly tired late sequels never managed. The connection to the original is real but unburdened. This is what a reboot should be, a transfusion rather than a reanimation, and the franchise feels, for the first time in years, like it has somewhere to go.

The remake of a horror classic falls into the trap that swallows nearly all of them, which is the assumption that better technology means better horror. The original frightened audiences with suggestion, with what the cheap effects of its era could not afford to show. The new film can afford to show everything, and shows it, and the explicitness drains away every drop of dread. Fear lives in the imagination, and this remake has spent its entire budget on leaving nothing to imagine.

The reboot is a perfectly competent film that I cannot summon any feeling about whatsoever. It does nothing wrong. It also does nothing, in the sense of adding any reason for its own existence. The story is told efficiently, the cast is fine, the production is glossy, and at no point did the picture suggest that anyone involved had a single passionate idea about why this particular franchise deserved to be revived now. It is the cinematic equivalent of a shrug, professionally executed.

The remake has done the genuinely difficult thing, which is to honour the original while disagreeing with it. The new film keeps the bones of the story but quietly reverses its sympathies, telling the same events from the side the original had cast as villains. It is a bold and respectful act of reinterpretation, and it sends you back to the original with fresh eyes. A remake this thoughtful is rare enough that I want to recommend the picture twice over.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The film rests almost entirely on the shoulders of its nine-year-old lead, and she carries it with a complete lack of strain. There is none of the precocious mugging that ruins so many child performances, none of the sense of a young actor performing cuteness for the camera. She simply is the character, attentive and uncertain and occasionally bored, and the director has had the wisdom to build the whole film around her unforced presence rather than around a plot.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The family film has become a debased category, a genre defined by what it carefully avoids rather than what it attempts, and this picture is a welcome rebuke to that timidity. It treats its young audience as intelligent. It allows its child characters to experience real fear, real loss, real moral difficulty, and it trusts that children can absorb a serious story. The result is a family film in the true sense, a film an actual family could watch together and afterwards have something to discuss.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The two child actors at the centre of this film have been directed into a register of genuine naturalism, and the achievement is considerable, because nothing is harder to coax from a young performer than ordinariness. They squabble the way real siblings squabble, with the specific repetitive grievances of children who share a room, and the picture's authenticity depends entirely on the rightness of that texture. It is a small film, and the children make it a true one.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The picture wants to be a heartwarming family adventure and is undone by a young lead who has plainly been directed to be adorable at all times. Every line is delivered with a calculated twinkle, every reaction is pitched for maximum audience sympathy, and the performance has the airless quality of a child being coached frame by frame. It is not the young actor's fault. It is a failure of direction, a failure to understand that a child on screen is most appealing when least aware of the camera.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: What this family film understands is that children are not a separate species requiring a separate, simpler kind of story. The picture's plot is genuinely complex, its emotional stakes are real, and its young protagonist is permitted to be wrong, to be unkind, to learn things slowly and imperfectly. The film respects its child characters enough to let them be difficult, and in doing so it respects its child audience enough to offer them something worth growing into.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The young performer at the centre of this picture does something I have rarely seen a child actor manage, which is to play a character genuinely thinking. There is a long scene near the end, almost wordless, in which she works through a difficult decision entirely in her face, and the camera trusts her to hold it, and she does. It is the kind of performance that makes you forget you are watching a performance, and the film is built, correctly, around the trust it places in her.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The family film has been assembled with one eye permanently on the merchandising opportunities, and the calculation is visible in every frame. The young characters are designed rather than written, each one a future toy, and the plot is a thin armature on which to hang a series of marketable set pieces. The child actors are doing what they can with it. But they have been hired to animate a product line, not to inhabit a story, and no amount of talent can disguise the difference.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The picture is a family film with the rare courage to be sad. It is about a child's first encounter with death, the death of a grandparent, and it does not rush the child through grief toward a tidy lesson. It lets the sadness sit. The young lead's performance is remarkable precisely because the director has not asked her to perform sadness but simply to be present within it, and the film earns its eventual, modest consolation honestly.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: The family adventure is loud, fast, and relentlessly busy, and it has been built on the apparent assumption that a child's attention can only be held by constant motion. The young cast is shouting most of their dialogue over a perpetual din of incident. There is no quiet anywhere in the film, no moment of stillness in which a child character might simply be, and the picture exhausts rather than entertains. Children deserve films that trust them to sit still, and this is not one of them.

subtopic: child performance and family film reviews
sentence: There is an entire history of cinema's failure with child actors, the mugging, the cuteness, the sense of a small adult performing a script, and this film stands as a quiet rebuke to all of it. The director has clearly worked patiently with her young lead, drawing out a performance of total naturalness, and the picture's emotional power flows directly from that authenticity. It is a small family film, and it contains the best child performance I have seen in a decade.

The score is the best thing in this otherwise unremarkable film, and it is doing so much narrative work that the picture would collapse without it. The composer has written a set of recurring themes that track the relationships between the characters with more precision than the screenplay manages, and there are emotional turns in the film that exist purely in the orchestration. It is a strange experience, watching a mediocre film carried almost entirely by its music, but the music is genuinely superb.

The film's score is a relentless act of emotional coercion. There is not a single moment in the picture that the music permits to be ambiguous. Sad scenes are scored sad, tense scenes are scored tense, and the orchestra arrives ahead of every feeling to instruct the audience exactly how to respond. A great score trusts the audience and leaves room for them. This one fills every silence with insistence, and the effect is less moving than bullying.

What I admired about this picture is its confidence to go without music. The director uses her score sparingly, perhaps four times across two hours, and the restraint means that when the orchestra finally does enter, the effect is overwhelming. The long unscored stretches teach the audience to listen to the film's actual sounds, the rooms and the weather and the breathing, and the eventual music lands like a held breath released. It is the most intelligent use of a film score I have heard in years.

The compiled soundtrack of period pop songs is doing the film no favours. Each needle-drop is so on-the-nose, so literally illustrative of the scene it accompanies, that the picture begins to feel like an extended advertisement for its own album. The songs are good songs. But a soundtrack is not a playlist, and a film that deploys its music this lazily, as mood-by-association rather than as genuine scoring, has abdicated one of cinema's most powerful tools.

The score, built almost entirely from processed and manipulated recordings of the human voice, is the most genuinely original film music I have encountered in a long time. The composer has refused the orchestra, refused the synthesiser, and constructed an entire sonic world from breath and hum and wordless singing. The effect is uncanny and intimate, and it gives the picture a texture no conventional score could provide. It is worth seeing the film for the sound alone.

The film has been scored in the current fashion, which is to say with a low ominous drone underneath nearly every scene, and the fashion is doing the picture real harm. The drone is meant to generate unease, and at first it does, but unease sustained without variation for two hours simply becomes a texture the ear tunes out. By the final act the score has lost all power to affect me, because it never once stopped, and a sound that never stops is, functionally, a silence.

The composer has written a score of genuine thematic intelligence, and the film's editors have, regrettably, chopped it to pieces. You can hear, in fragments, the shape of the music the composer intended, melodic lines that begin and are cut off, developments that are interrupted by a scene change. The score deserved a film cut to accommodate it. Instead it has been treated as wallpaper, trimmed to fit, and a fine piece of musical writing has been reduced to a series of stings.

The picture's use of silence is its boldest musical decision. The composer was apparently instructed to write a full score and then, in the edit, the director removed nearly all of it, leaving the film's most harrowing sequences to play out in total quiet. The absence is devastating. We are denied the orchestral cushion that would tell us how to feel, and forced to sit with the images unguided, and the discomfort is precisely the point. A score, sometimes, is most powerful when it has been taken away.

The score is generic in the specific contemporary way, the kind of anonymous orchestral wash that could be lifted from this film and dropped into a dozen others without anyone noticing. There is no theme to remember, no instrumental colour that belongs to this story and no other. The composer is plainly capable of better; the film has simply asked for the safe default, the audio equivalent of beige, and the music does its job and leaves no trace.

There is a single musical idea in this film that justifies the whole picture. The composer has written a simple four-note motif, introduced quietly in the opening scene, and across two hours it is transformed, inverted, slowed, and finally, in the closing moments, resolved, and the resolution carries an emotional weight that the screenplay alone could never have reached. It is a master class in how a film score can tell a story underneath the story, and it deserves to be studied.

The picture has been shot by a cinematographer at the height of her powers, and the images are so beautiful that they nearly compensate for a screenplay that has nothing to say. Light is used here as a genuine narrative element, the colour temperature shifting with the protagonist's circumstances, the framing growing more constricted as his options narrow. I could watch this film with the sound off and follow the emotional arc entirely. With the sound on, unfortunately, the dialogue keeps intruding.

The film has been graded into a murky teal-and-orange palette so aggressively that the actors' faces have taken on the colour of corrosion. This is the house style of modern studio cinema, and I have come to loathe it. It flattens every location into the same dim sludge, drains the world of any colour that might distinguish one scene from another, and signifies, falsely, a kind of seriousness. The picture is not serious. It is merely badly lit, and proud of it.

What distinguishes this film visually is its commitment to the static frame. The camera almost never moves. Scene after scene is composed as a fixed tableau, and the viewer's eye is left to travel within the image rather than being led around it by the director. It is an old-fashioned discipline, and it asks more of the audience than the modern restless camera does, but the rewards are real. Every frame here has been genuinely composed, and composition, properly done, is its own kind of storytelling.

The picture has been shot on film rather than digitally, and the difference is not nostalgic affectation but a genuine aesthetic argument. The grain gives the image a living texture, a faint perpetual motion within every frame, and the way film handles the highlights, the soft bloom around a window or a lamp, lends the picture a warmth that digital crispness cannot replicate. The story is slight. The look is a sustained pleasure, and the look, here, is most of the point.

The film's visual style is all surface and no thought. The cinematographer has clearly been given a free hand, and the result is a picture drunk on its own technique, swooping crane shots and ostentatious lens flares and a colour palette that changes for no discernible reason. None of it means anything. The camera moves because the camera can move, and the visual restlessness, untethered from the story, becomes simply tiring. Style must serve something. This style serves only itself.

There is a sequence in this picture, a slow push across a rain-soaked courtyard at dusk, that contains more genuine feeling than the entire screenplay. The cinematographer has understood the emotional content of the scene better than the writer did, and has built an image, the wet stone, the failing light, the single lit window, that carries the loneliness the dialogue keeps fumbling. It is a reminder that cinema is, finally, a visual medium, and that a great image can rescue a weak page.

The picture has been shot almost entirely in extreme close-up, and the choice, sustained for two hours, becomes genuinely oppressive. We are never permitted to see a room, a landscape, a body in full; we are pressed against faces and hands and fragments for the entire running time. I understand the intention, an intimacy bordering on suffocation, and for twenty minutes it is effective. For two hours it is a punishment, and I left the cinema craving the simple relief of a wide shot.

What the cinematography achieves here is a genuine sense of place. The film is set in a single northern town, and the camera has been used to make us feel the specific quality of that town's light, the low winter sun, the long shadows, the particular grey of the sky. By the end of the film I felt I had visited a real location rather than a set, and that conviction is the cinematographer's quiet achievement, the kind that wins no awards because it never draws attention to itself.

The film is visually incoherent in a way that suggests a production with no controlling eye. Some scenes are lit with care; others appear to have been shot with whatever was available. The colour grading shifts without motivation. The framing is sometimes precise and sometimes careless. A film can have an ugly visual style and still be unified, but this picture has no style at all, only a sequence of visual decisions made, scene by scene, by people who were not consulting one another.

The picture has been shot in black and white, and for once the choice is not a gesture toward prestige but a genuine necessity of the material. The story is about memory, and the absence of colour gives every image the quality of something already past, already being remembered. The cinematographer has used the monochrome to sculpt with light and shadow in a way colour would have softened, and the result is a film that looks the way the act of remembering actually feels.

The film has been made for streaming, and it bears all the marks of the format's particular pathologies. It is too long, because length is now a metric of value, and it has been edited with the assumption that the viewer is doing something else, every plot point restated two or three times so that nobody glancing at their phone will lose the thread. There may be a tight ninety-minute film inside this bloated two-hour-twenty one, but the economics of streaming actively discourage anyone from finding it.

It is genuinely strange to watch a film of this quality dropped onto a streaming service with no fanfare, no theatrical run, no sense of occasion. The picture deserves a cinema. The cinematography is built for a large screen, the sound design rewards a proper system, and the slow, patient storytelling demands the kind of uninterrupted attention that a living room rarely provides. It will be watched in fragments, on laptops, half-attended, and a real film will be quietly diminished by the manner of its release.

The streaming film has been algorithmically assembled from the components of past successes, and watching it is like watching a survey of audience preferences rendered as drama. The premise tests well. The cast has been chosen for their separate fan bases. The runtime is calibrated to the platform's retention data. It is a competent, frictionless, entirely soulless product, and it will perform exactly as projected, and nobody will remember a frame of it a week later, which is, one suspects, fine by everyone who made it.

What this streaming release proves is that the format can still, occasionally, enable real ambition. The film is the kind of mid-budget adult drama that the theatrical market has all but abandoned, and it exists only because a streaming service was willing to fund it. The picture is patient, intelligent, and aimed squarely at grown-ups, and for all my reservations about the streaming model, I have to concede that without it this particular good film would simply not have been made.

The film has the unmistakable visual flatness of a production lit and shot for the small screen. The compositions are simple, the close-ups frequent, the lighting bright and even, all of it optimised for legibility on a phone rather than beauty on a wall. There is nothing wrong with making a film for the screen most people will actually watch it on. The constraints of the budget are visible in every frame, and the director has had the wisdom not to hide them. The film wears its poverty openly, and the openness becomes a kind of honesty, a refusal of the gloss that more expensive pictures use to flatter their audiences. It is a rough, immediate, deeply felt piece of work, and its roughness is not a flaw to be excused but a texture to be valued.

It is genuinely thrilling to watch a film succeed on resourcefulness alone. This picture had no money for a second take, no money for a crane, no money for anything but the bare essentials, and the bare essentials, it turns out, were enough. The director and her tiny crew have made something that feels complete and confident and entirely uncompromised, and they have done it on a budget that would embarrass a wedding video.

The small-budget film is often praised in a slightly condescending register, as a brave little effort, and I want to avoid that register entirely, because this picture deserves better than condescension. It is one of the three or four best films I have seen this year, and its budget is a piece of trivia, not an excuse. The triumph here is not that they made a film cheaply. The triumph is that they made a film this good.

With no money for distraction, this film simply sits down with its characters and listens to them, for ninety minutes, and the listening is riveting. There is no score to tell you how to feel, no production design to admire, no movement the budget could not afford. There is only writing and acting and attention, and the picture is a quiet reminder that those three things, and nothing else, have always been the actual art of cinema.

The picture proves, yet again, a truth the industry seems determined to forget, that the relationship between a film's budget and its quality is essentially nil. This tiny film, made by unknowns for the price of a modest car, is funnier, sadder, and more memorable than the bloated tentpole I reviewed last week. The money buys spectacle. It cannot buy the things that actually matter, and this small triumph is the proof.

The film takes on a subject that most pictures would not dare to approach, and the courage of the attempt deserves acknowledgement before anything else. Whether the film handles the material responsibly is a separate and harder question, and my answer is a qualified yes. The director has resisted both sensationalism and false comfort, and the result is genuinely difficult to watch, which is, given the subject, exactly as it should be.

There is a real risk, in dramatising a subject this raw, of producing something that exploits the very pain it claims to examine, and this film does not entirely avoid the trap. There are sequences staged for an impact that tips over into spectacle, moments where the camera lingers in a way that serves the audience's appetite rather than the story's need. The picture is serious. It is also, in places, not as careful as its subject demanded.

The film addresses a subject that has become almost impossible to address without controversy, and it does so with a clear-eyed sobriety that I found admirable. It does not editorialise. It does not soften. It presents its difficult material with a documentary steadiness and trusts the audience to bring their own conscience to it, and that trust is, in the current climate, an act of genuine artistic nerve.

I am uneasy about this film, and the unease is not a criticism so much as a description of what the picture is for. It takes a subject most people would prefer not to think about and refuses to let the audience look away, and the discomfort I felt was plainly intended. A film about this material that left me comfortable would have failed. This one succeeds, if success is the word, by being almost unbearable.

The picture handles its inflammatory subject with a restraint that some viewers will mistake for timidity, and they will be wrong. The restraint is the point. The director has understood that the loudest possible treatment of this material would also be the cheapest, and she has chosen instead a quiet, exact, deeply considered approach that respects the gravity of the subject far more than any sensational version could.

The controversy around this film has, predictably, focused on whether the subject should be dramatised at all, and that is the least interesting question available. The subject can be dramatised. The question is whether it has been dramatised well, and on that the answer is mixed, a screenplay of real intelligence undermined by a director who too often reaches for shock when patience would have served better.

The film walks a genuinely difficult line, dramatising a subject around which any misstep would be disastrous, and it walks that line with remarkable poise. It neither flinches from the horror nor wallows in it. It gives the people at the centre of the story their full humanity rather than reducing them to the issue they represent, and that refusal of reduction is the picture's quiet, considerable moral achievement.

It is a brave film about a subject most filmmakers would not touch, and bravery, I have to note, is not the same thing as wisdom. The picture's intentions are unimpeachable, and its execution is frequently questionable, staging its most painful material with a frankness that crosses, more than once, from honesty into something closer to assault. The subject deserved this film's seriousness. It did not deserve this film's lapses of judgement.

The film tackles its difficult subject without offering the audience the consolations the subject usually comes wrapped in. There is no redemptive arc, no uplift, no sense that the suffering has been made to mean something. The director has refused all of it, and the refusal is harsh and honest and correct, because the false comfort would have been a lie, and a lie about this particular subject would have been unforgivable.

What the film does with its controversial material is, finally, to humanise it, and that is harder and rarer than the controversy around the picture suggests. It would have been easy to make this subject into an issue, a debate, a position to be argued. The director has instead made it into people, specific and flawed and impossible to reduce to a slogan, and in doing so she has made the only kind of film about this subject that was worth making.

For two acts this is an exceptional film, and I want that on the record before I describe what goes wrong, because for two acts it is genuinely exceptional. The characters are rich, the situation is gripping, the direction is assured. And then the third act arrives, and the picture, as if seized by panic, abandons everything it had built in favour of a frantic mechanical resolution that belongs to a much worse film.

The third-act problem is the most common failure mode in modern screenwriting, and this picture is a clinical example of it. The first hour establishes a complex web of relationships with real care. The final half-hour has to resolve that web, and it does so by simply cutting every knot at once, a flurry of confrontations and revelations and tidyings-up that no preceding scene had earned. The setup deserved a payoff. It got a cleanup.

There is a structural law that the third act must deliver on the promises of the first, and this film breaks the law spectacularly. The promises made in the opening act are subtle and human; the third act delivers, instead, a series of loud incidents that answer questions nobody was asking. It is as though two different screenwriters worked on the picture and never met, and the one who wrote the ending had not read the beginning.

The picture has a third-act problem of an unusual kind, which is that it does not seem to want a third act at all. The first two acts build toward a confrontation, and then, at the moment the confrontation should arrive, the film simply declines it, drifting instead toward a vague and unsatisfying dissolution. I admire a film that resists easy resolution. I am less sure I admire a film that resists resolution altogether.

Everything wrong with this film is in its final twenty minutes. Strike them, and you would have a small, sharp, satisfying picture. As released, the film spends those final twenty minutes explaining itself, an exhausting sequence of expository confrontations in which characters tell each other, and us, what the preceding ninety minutes had already shown with perfect clarity. The third act does not advance the film. It annotates it.

The third act is where this film loses its nerve. For most of its length the picture has trusted the audience, withholding judgement, leaving its moral questions genuinely open. Then, in the final stretch, it suddenly decides it must tell us what to think, and the ending arrives with a heavy explanatory thud, closing every door the film had so intelligently left ajar. A braver final act would have left us in the doorway.

It is a familiar disappointment, the film that cannot land its ending, and this picture is a particularly painful instance because the first two acts are so good. The director has clearly understood the human material beautifully and the plot mechanics not at all, and the third act is all plot mechanics, a clattering apparatus of twists and reversals grinding toward a resolution that satisfies the diagram and betrays the people.

The third-act problem here is one of pace. The film spends two acts in an unhurried, observational register, and then the final act, as if suddenly aware of the running time, accelerates wildly, compressing what should have been the picture's richest material into a breathless sprint. The ending the film wanted is in there somewhere. It has simply been delivered at three times the speed the rest of the picture established.

The picture stumbles, as so many do, at the third-act resolution, and the specific stumble is a failure of belief. The film does not believe its audience will accept an unhappy ending, and so it manufactures a hopeful one, a final scene of unearned reconciliation that contradicts everything the preceding two hours had honestly established. The film knew what its true ending was. It lost the courage to film it.

There is so much to admire in this film that its third-act collapse is genuinely painful to report. The screenplay, so precise and patient through its opening, simply disintegrates in the final reel into a series of contrivances, the long-lost letter, the timely confession, the coincidental meeting. The film had been better than this. It had spent two acts proving it was better than this, and then, at the finish, it settled.

The film arrives draped in the unmistakable costume of awards-season ambition, the weighty subject, the transformative performances, the tasteful restraint, and the costume fits a little too perfectly. Every element has been calibrated to a campaign rather than a story. The picture is accomplished, certainly, but it has the airless quality of a film made to be nominated, and I admired it the way one admires a well-filled-out form.

What distinguishes this prestige contender from the season's other strivers is that it seems genuinely unaware of its own awards potential. It is a serious film about a serious subject, and yet it never strikes the calculated poses, never pauses for the speech that exists to be clipped into a ceremony reel. The seriousness is real rather than performed, and that authenticity, in this season of campaigns, is itself remarkable.

The picture has been positioned, with some confidence, as the front-runner, and having seen it I find the confidence misplaced. The film is handsome and well-acted and utterly without surprise, a procession of the exact scenes the prestige drama is contractually required to provide. It will be nominated. It will probably win things. And it will be forgotten faster than the messier, braver films it is about to defeat.

There is a long lead performance at the centre of this contender, the kind that involves a visible physical transformation and a great deal of suffering, and it is being discussed as a certainty for the major prizes. The performance is, in fact, very good. It is also exactly the performance the season rewards every year, and I found myself wishing the actor had been given something subtler to do than to be obviously, awardably excellent.

The film is the season's designated important picture, and the designation has done it no favours. You can feel the weight of expectation pressing down on every frame, the sense of a film straining to be worthy, and the strain has squeezed out the spontaneity that the same director's smaller, unheralded work possesses in abundance. The contender is impressive. It is also, somehow, less alive than the films nobody is campaigning for.

For once, the prestige contender deserves its prestige. The film could easily have been the usual tasteful awards-season fare, given the subject, and instead the director has made something genuinely searching, a picture that uses the conventions of the serious drama as a starting point rather than a destination. It will compete for prizes, and for once I will not begrudge it the trophies, because the film underneath the campaign is the real thing.

The picture has every marker of the awards contender, and watching it is a slightly eerie experience, like meeting a person assembled from a checklist. Here is the historical importance. Here is the social relevance. Here is the showcase monologue, lit and framed for the highlight reel. The film is competent at every individual thing it does, and the sum of all that competence is a strange hollowness, a film that exists to be honoured rather than seen.

The awards-season contender has been released in the prestige slot, late in the year, with the full apparatus of a campaign behind it, and the apparatus is louder than the film. The picture itself is a modest, decent drama that would, in spring, have been received as a modest, decent drama. Inflated to the dimensions of a front-runner, it cannot help but disappoint, and the disappointment is the campaign's fault, not the film's.

It is the kind of serious-minded prestige picture that critics are expected to either champion or resent, and I find I can do neither, because the film is too well-made to dismiss and too predictable to celebrate. It is a thoroughly professional act of awards-season filmmaking, and its professionalism is precisely the limit. A great film takes a risk. This one has taken a position, and a position, however noble, is not the same thing as art.

The contender's campaign has worked, and the film is now spoken of in the hushed tones reserved for the season's anointed, and I want to gently dissent. The picture is good. It is not great. It is a polished, sincere, intelligent drama that has been promoted into a significance it cannot quite sustain, and when the ceremonies are over and the campaign has gone quiet, what will remain is simply a good film, which would have been enough.
